name: Buy out repeatedly flooded homes and return the land to open space
trigger: A block group has at least one unmitigated NFIP Severe Repetitive Loss home (nfipSrl = true) or two or more Repetitive Loss homes (nfipRl = true), with mitigatedIndicator = false, a residential occupancyType (1-3, 11-16) and a rated floodZone of A* or V*. Optional extra condition: the block group intersects the NFHL Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA_TF = 'T'). Floodway areas (ZONE_SUBTY = 'FLOODWAY') rank first.
trigger_data:
Main dataset: OpenFEMA 'NFIP Multiple Loss Properties' v1 (FEMA).
- Contents: one record per NFIP repetitive-loss structure, with censusBlockGroup (12-digit 2020 block group, geocoded), fipsCountyCode, communityIdNumber, floodZone, nfipRl, nfipSrl, mitigatedIndicator, insuredIndicator, totalLosses and occupancyType. FEMA describes it as: 'This dataset provides information on structures that have had multiple National Flood Insurance (NFIP) claims across the history of the program.'
- API: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v1/NfipMultipleLossProperties (CSV and JSON). Metadata: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v1/DataSets?$filter=name%20eq%20%27NfipMultipleLossProperties%27
- Updated: metadata 'modified' 2025-12-05.
- Terms: OpenFEMA Terms and Conditions, https://www.fema.gov/about/openfema/terms-conditions. The metadata points to this page, but it returned HTTP 403 and I could not read it.
- Caveats: latitude and longitude are cut to 1 decimal place, and FEMA warns that block-group assignment is geocoded and has error.

Flood zone layer: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL), layer 28 'Flood Hazard Zones' (FLD_ZONE, ZONE_SUBTY, SFHA_TF), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28. It is a live service covering every area FEMA has digitized. The data.gov NFHL record (https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/national-flood-hazard-layer-nfhl, a HIFLD copy last updated 2022-10-24) lists the license https://www.usa.gov/government-works.
effect:
Effect on nearby home values: negative for adjacent homes in the short run.
- New York coastal counties, post-Sandy NY Rising program: homes sold within 100 m of a buyout or acquisition sold for 10-20% less.
- For buyouts the drop fades after 100 m. The effect approaches zero about 4 years after the program starts and may turn positive after 5 years (Hashida & Dundas 2023).
- Other studies disagree, so treat the sign as uncertain (see notes).
- Safety benefit: the bought-out home is permanently removed from future flood losses.
effect_source: Hashida, Yukiko & Dundas, Steven J. (2023). The effects of a voluntary property buyout and acquisition program on coastal housing markets: Evidence from New York. Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 121, DOI 10.1016/j.jeem.2023.102873. I read the publisher abstract on IDEAS/RePEc because ScienceDirect blocked automated access.
effect_quote: Both a repeat sales difference-in-differences approach and an event study addressing treatment effect heterogeneity suggest that buyouts and acquisitions have sizable negative effects on prices (−20 to −10 percent) for homes sold adjacent (≤100 m) to participating properties. The spatial scale of the impacts differs across policy types, with negative effects attenuating after 100 m for buyouts but persisting for acquisitions up to 1200 m.
cost:
Unit cost: the pre-flood fair market value of the home, plus about $23,000 per property in local and state government activity costs (about 18% of the purchase price).
- Source: median buyout project in a 2020 survey of North Carolina local officials and state hazard mitigation officers nationwide (Curran-Groome et al. 2022, Land Use Policy 118:106128).
- Map formula: local median home value × about 1.18.
- Example from a high-cost market: New York's post-Sandy direct buyout cost was $274.86 million for 723 buyouts, about $380,000 each (my calculation; see notes).
cost_quote: Respondents reported that activity costs at the local and state government levels account for approximately $23,000 per property for the median buyout project, or roughly 18% of property purchase costs.
research_notes:
Other neighbor-effect estimates (they conflict):
- Guo, Liao & Miao (2023), RFF Working Paper 23-44, https://media.rff.org/documents/WP_23-44.pdf. It studies the same NY program: 'Our baseline specification in column (1) indicates that a home acquisition or buyout significantly increases property values within a 1 km radius by 3.66 percent.' However, for buyouts alone: 'In contrast, the effects of buyouts are much smaller and become negligible after 100 m.' RFF has also posted an updated version, which I did not read.
- Lee et al. (2023), Lincoln Institute WP23RJL1, Harris County, TX, https://storage.pardot.com/153411/1693934548kDKfVk8S/Lee_WP23RJL1.pdf: 'Specifically, it shows that an increase in buyout properties within any range of a buffer would decrease property values by a range of 0.12 to 0.60% per buyout.'
- Hashida & Dundas, same abstract: 'These impacts are shown to approach zero four years after policy initiation, and the effect of buyouts may turn positive after five years.'

Purchase price: CRS Insight IN11911, https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2025-04-22_IN11911_86c088b43111aba7e95b4fc73d2c6f71a79a91a3.html: 'Homeowners are generally offered the pre-disaster fair market value of the property.' The same Insight says the local government must maintain the bought-out lots.

NY example, from the RFF paper: 'the direct cost of buyouts was $274.86 million' and 'Participating properties totaled 1,289, of which 566 were acquisitions and 723 buyouts.'

FEMA benchmark: FEMA's September 2021 pre-calculated benefits memo, https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_acquisition-elevation-precalculated-benefits-memo_092021.pdf, lists 'Acquisitions: $323,000 per structure'. Acquisitions in the 1% flood zone whose total project cost is at or below this are treated as cost-effective. This is an average-benefit (avoided loss) ceiling, not a price. I read the memo earlier in this run, but later re-fetches got HTTP 403. https://floodready.vermont.gov/node/832 restates: 'The 2021 pre-calculated values are $323,000 and $205,000 respectively.'

Scale (Mach et al. 2019, Science Advances, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6785245/): 'From 1989 to 2017, FEMA funded 43,633 voluntary buyouts of flood-prone properties for which data are publicly available'.

Policy note: Lee et al. find tree canopy offsets part of the loss. Pair buyouts with maintained green space so the lots do not become a vacant-lot discount.

name: Elevate flood-prone homes and roads
trigger:
Residential buildings inside the NFHL Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA_TF = 'T'; FLD_ZONE A, AE, AH, AO or VE) built before the community's first flood map (pre-FIRM).
- Rule: FEMA counts a building as post-FIRM if construction or substantial improvement started after 31 Dec 1974 or on/after the community's initial FIRM date, whichever is later.
- Block-group measure: count NFIP policies with postFIRMConstructionIndicator = false (or preFIRMConstructionIndicator = true) and floodZoneCurrent in the SFHA, grouped by censusGeoid.
- Exclude homes already flagged for buyout (Severe Repetitive Loss).
trigger_data:
1) FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28. Live service, nationwide where digitized. License: https://www.usa.gov/government-works, per https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/national-flood-hazard-layer-nfhl.

2) OpenFEMA 'NFIP Community Status Book' v1, https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v1/NfipCommunityStatusBook. One row per NFIP community. Its field initialFloodInsuranceRateMap is, in FEMA's words, the 'dividing line between two building categories called Pre-FIRM and Post-FIRM'. Metadata modified 2026-07-28.

3) OpenFEMA 'NFIP Redacted Policies' v3, https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v3/NfipPolicies. Includes postFIRMConstructionIndicator and floodZoneCurrent, with censusGeoid 'presented at the Census Block Group level'. Metadata modified 2026-10-14.

Terms for 2 and 3: OpenFEMA Terms and Conditions, https://www.fema.gov/about/openfema/terms-conditions. The page returned HTTP 403 and I did not read it.
effect:
Effect on home values: no resale premium measured.
- Charleston, SC: repeated floods slowed appreciation, and elevated homes lost more appreciation than non-elevated homes. The market did not value elevation (Blackwell, Mothorpe & Wright 2024). The abstract gives no percentage.
- Safety and cost (Jefferson Parish, LA): raising existing homes 3 ft above ground or to the base flood elevation, whichever is higher, cut median average annual flood loss by 98%. Benefit-cost ratio: 1.5 over 30 years, 1.7 over 70 years (Al Assi et al. 2023; see notes).
effect_source: Blackwell, Calvin; Mothorpe, Chris; Wright, Julie (2024). Flooding and Elevation: An Examination of Differential Price Responses to Flood Events. Journal of Sustainable Real Estate 16(1), 2372133, DOI 10.1080/19498276.2024.2372133. I read the abstract on IDEAS/RePEc; tandfonline.com returned HTTP 403.
effect_quote: We find flooding significantly reduces the rate of appreciation, and home elevation increases the rate of lost appreciation. Our results suggest home elevation is not a flood risk adaptation and mitigation strategy valued by the market.
cost: About $120,000 per single-family home: the average elevation cost set by Louisiana GOHSEP for Jefferson Parish, LA, after the 2005 storms. FEMA's HMGP grant paid about $90,000 and Louisiana's Road Home grant about $30,000.
cost_quote: The cost of elevating homes in the selected study area (i.e., $120,000) was determined by GOHSEP. Because the HMGP grants typically cover 75% of the cost, while The Road Home Program grants cover the remaining 25%, the HMGP and Road Home Program grants typically provide $90,000 and $30,000 per home, respectively.
cost_check: failed: Verifiable alternative wording (Research Square preprint v1, 12 Oct 2022, https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-2126597/latest.pdf): 'The total elevation cost per existing home in the presented case study area is approximately $120,000, with around 25% ($30,000) being the Road Home Program share.'
research_notes:
Cost source: Al Assi, Mostafiz, Friedland, Rohli, Taghinezhad & Rahim (2023), Cost-effectiveness of federal CDBG-DR Road Home Program mitigation assistance in Jefferson Parish, Louisiana. Natural Hazards 117:1291-1319, DOI 10.1007/s11069-023-05904-3, open access. Springer served a bot-check page when I re-fetched it; I had read the full article earlier in this run.

Safety and cost quotes from the same paper:
- 'The analysis reveals that elevating existing homes by either 3 feet above the ground or to the base flood elevation (BFE; 100-year flood elevation), whichever is higher, reduces the median AAL by 98%.'
- 'This elevation generates a BCR of 1.5 and 1.7 over a 30-year mortgage and a 70-year building lifetime, respectively, if the benefit is allocated proportionately.'

Other cost benchmarks:
- Reguero et al. (2018), PLoS ONE, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5894966/. Their Gulf-wide model prices raising homes 10 ft at '$83,300 / house' and finds a benefit-cost ratio of only 0.41-0.73 for home elevation across the Gulf.
- FEMA 2021 pre-calculated benefits memo: 'Elevations (and Mitigation Reconstruction3): $205,000 per structure'. This is a benefit ceiling for cost-effectiveness, not a price.

Roads: I found no cost or effect source for road elevation in this pass.

name: Living shoreline, dune or wetland restoration
trigger:
A block group touches a shoreline inside FEMA coastal flood zones: NFHL FLD_ZONE 'V' or 'VE', or seaward of the Limit of Moderate Wave Action line (Coastal A zone). Which project to suggest:
- Sheltered estuary, bay, river, sound or Great Lakes shore: living shoreline or marsh.
- Open-ocean beach (V/VE, or where the Primary Frontal Dunes layer is mapped): dune.
- Rank by FEMA National Risk Index coastal-flooding expected annual loss (CFLD_EALB).
trigger_data:
FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer MapServer, https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer. Layers used:
- 28 Flood Hazard Zones (FLD_ZONE V/VE)
- 19 Limit of Moderate Wave Action (landward edge of Coastal A)
- 25 Primary Frontal Dunes
- 0 NFHL Availability (coverage)
Live service, nationwide where digitized. License: https://www.usa.gov/government-works, per https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/national-flood-hazard-layer-nfhl (HIFLD copy last updated 2022-10-24).

Ranking: FEMA National Risk Index Census Tracts, https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Census_Tracts/FeatureServer. Fields CFLD_EALB and CFLD_RISKR. 'National Risk Index Data Version: December 2025 (1.20.0)'. Terms are in the item's licenseInfo, https://www.arcgis.com/sharing/rest/content/items/9da4eeb936544335a6db0cd7a8448a51?f=json: planning use only, and a citation statement is required.
effect:
Dunes, home values: building dunes raised New Jersey coastal home prices by about 3.6% net. Lost ocean views and privacy partly offset the protection benefit (Dundas 2017).

Wetlands and marshes: no home-value estimate found. Measured damage reduction: wetlands avoided about $625 million of direct flood damage in Hurricane Sandy across 12 states. Homes behind a salt marsh in Barnegat Bay, NJ had 16% lower annual flood losses (Narayan et al. 2017).
effect_source: Dundas, Steven J. (2017). Benefits and ancillary costs of natural infrastructure: Evidence from the New Jersey coast. Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 85: 62-80, DOI 10.1016/j.jeem.2017.04.008. I read the abstract on IDEAS/RePEc; ScienceDirect blocked automated access.
effect_quote: I identify the net effect of treatment utilizing the doubly robust Oaxaca-Blinder estimator and show that coastal housing price increases attributable to constructed dunes are approximately 3.6%.
cost: $300 to more than $1,500 per linear foot of living shoreline, depending on wave energy and technique (Maryland Department of Natural Resources, May 2026).
cost_quote: A living shoreline can range from $300 to over $1,500 per linear foot, depending on the wave energy environment and technique utilized.
research_notes:
Siting rule (NOAA Fisheries, https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/insight/understanding-living-shorelines): 'Estuaries, bays, rivers, and other sheltered shorelines are good candidates for living shorelines. Typically, living shorelines are not found on beaches along the open ocean.' NOAA also says living shorelines 'tend to cost less than hardened shorelines, for both installation and maintenance.'

Dundas also finds a cost to views: 'A decomposition of the average impact suggests that the policy intervention generates ancillary costs related to impaired ocean views and privacy concerns that partially offset large protection benefits.'

Narayan et al. (2017), Scientific Reports 7:9463, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-017-09269-z:
- 'Using an extensive database of property exposure, the regional study shows that wetlands avoided $625 Million in direct flood damages during Hurricane Sandy.'
- 'Properties behind a marsh, on average, save 16% in flood losses every year compared to properties where marshes have been lost.'

Other cost figures (they vary widely):
- Maryland DNR FAQ for local governments (2013 PDF), https://dnr.maryland.gov/ccs/Documents/ls/FAQs_LocalGovernments.pdf: 'a living shoreline project generally costs between $200 and $400 per linear foot'.
- Delaware DNREC I-ADAPT sheet (2022 dollars), https://documents.dnrec.delaware.gov/I-ADAPT/AdaptationStrategies/Living%20Shorelines.pdf: contractor design plus construction at $1,000-$5,000 per linear foot (from a table).
- Reguero et al. (2018), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5894966/: $25 M/mile for salt-marsh restoration and $1.5 M/mile for oyster reefs. They conclude: 'Nature-based adaptation options could avert more than $50 billion of these costs, and do so cost effectively with average benefit to cost ratios above 3.5.'

name: Stronger wind code and fortified-roof grants
trigger:
The county is in the hurricane-prone region per FEMA's Building Code Adoption Tracking (BCAT) data (Hurricane_Risk = 'T').
- Suggest a building-code upgrade where Hurricane_Resistance is 'Not Resistant' or 'Partially Resistant'.
- Suggest FORTIFIED Roof grants in tracts with National Risk Index hurricane rating HRCN_RISKR of 'Very High' or 'Relatively High'.
- The mapping step's ASCE 7 design wind speed of 130 mph or more cannot be applied from open data (ASCE 7 maps are not an open national dataset). The Alabama report supports 130 mph as the line above which the 2021+ residential code nearly matches FORTIFIED (see notes).
trigger_data:
1) FEMA Building Code Adoption Tracking (BCAT) Counties, ArcGIS feature service https://services.arcgis.com/DN2fPfpggEPlLhP6/arcgis/rest/services/FEMA_Building_Code_Adoptions_Tracking_Counties/FeatureServer/0. Item metadata: https://www.arcgis.com/sharing/rest/content/items/dcd25a0db911410cbbb07d4c984ff54e?f=json.
- Geography: county, all 50 states, DC and 5 territories. Fields include Hurricane_Risk (T/F), Hurricane_Resistance and Wind_Risk. Description: 'Tracked hazards include: flood, seismic, damaging wind, hurricane wind, and tornado.'
- Updated: Data_Currency 2025-12-31; item modified 2026-02-03.
- License: 'This work is marked with CC0 1.0'.

2) FEMA National Risk Index Census Tracts, https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Census_Tracts/FeatureServer. Fields HRCN_RISKR, HRCN_EALB and HRCN_AFREQ. Data Version December 2025 (1.20.0). Terms (item licenseInfo): 'The National Risk Index data are meant for planning purposes only.' A citation statement is required.
effect:
Effect on home values (coastal Alabama):
- FORTIFIED-designated homes sold for about 2-4% more, from sales 2011-2021 (Petrolia et al. 2023).
- A second peer-reviewed study finds a 6-7% premium at median distance to the coast, highest nearest the coast (Awondo et al. 2023; see notes).

Losses:
- Hurricane Sally (2020, Alabama): FORTIFIED homes had 55-74% fewer claims and 14-40% smaller claims (ALDOI/UA CRIR 2025).
- Florida's 2001 statewide code cut windstorm losses by up to 72%, returning $6 of avoided loss per $1 of added cost (Simmons et al. 2018).
effect_source: Petrolia, Daniel; Ishee, Shea; Yun, Seong; Cummings, Reid; Maples, Josh (2023). Do Wind Hazard Mitigation Programs Affect Home Sales Values? Journal of Real Estate Research 45(2): 137-159, DOI 10.1080/08965803.2022.2066249. I read the abstract on EconPapers.
effect_quote: The results of our full- and nearest-neighbor-matched sample design suggest a likely price premium significance on the order of 2-4% for FORTIFIED homes.
cost: About $13,000 average per FORTIFIED Roof retrofit in Alabama's Strengthen Alabama Homes program, which pays up to $10,000 per roof (figures as of 12 Nov 2024; about 8,700 homes retrofitted with about $86 million paid).
cost_quote: SAH pays up to $10,000 per roof. The average cost of retrofitting a house in the SAH program is about $13,000.
research_notes:
Second resale study: Awondo, Hollans, Powell & Wade (2023), Estimating the effects of wind loss mitigation on home value. Southern Economic Journal 90(1): 71-89. Abstract: https://ideas.repec.org/a/wly/soecon/v90y2023i1p71-89.html. Quote: 'We find that on average homebuyers located at median distance to the coast pay a 6%–7% premium for Fortified homes, which exceeds the typical cost of building or retrofitting houses to the Fortified standard.'

From the ALDOI and UA Center for Risk and Insurance Research report (May 2025, same PDF as the cost):
- Claims: 'Depending on the selected designation, sample, and measure, Fortified construction reduced loss frequency by 55% to 74%, loss severity by 14% to 40%, and loss ratio by 51% to 72%.'
- Insurance: Alabama's required wind-premium discounts 'range from 50% for new Fortified Gold houses to 20% for Fortified Roof designations earned more than five years earlier.'
- 130 mph line: 'In areas which have adopted the latest IRC (2021 and soon 2024) with a design wind speed above 130 mph, the code now closely mirrors the IBHS Fortified standard.'
- Extra cost, cited second-hand (I did not open Ghosh et al.): 'Estimates of the increased cost range from 0.5% to 3% for new construction to the Fortified Gold level, and 6% to 16% for retrofitting an existing home to the Fortified Roof standard (Ghosh et al. 2023).'

Building code: Simmons, Czajkowski & Done (2018), Land Economics 94(2): 155-174, https://le.uwpress.org/content/94/2/155. Quote: 'We use 10 years of paid insured loss data to show that the FBC reduced windstorm losses by up to 72%, then use our results to conduct a benefit-cost analysis (BCA). The FBC passes the BCA by a margin of $6 in full reduced loss to $1 of added cost, with a payback period of approximately 8 years.'

Grant terms (https://strengthenalabamahomes.com/): 'Grants will pay 100% of the cost of mitigation up to $10,000'.

trigger: A block group whose streets lie inside an NFHL 1% flood zone (SFHA_TF = 'T') or 0.2% flood zone (FLD_ZONE = 'X' with ZONE_SUBTY = '0.2 PCT ANNUAL CHANCE FLOOD HAZARD'). effect:
Grey storm-drain upgrades: no home-value effect measured; I found no study.

Green stormwater infrastructure (bioswales, rain gardens, tree trenches), Philadelphia: houses within 25 m of a completed site sold for about 10% more per square foot than houses near planned sites. The premium falls to 5-6% at 40 m and 3% at 50 m (Cohen, Huang & McMillen 2024, working paper).

effect_quote: Houses that are within 25m of a completed GSI sell at a premium of about 10 percent in price per-square foot compared with houses that are within a planned GSI location.
cost: Grey: about $500 per linear foot of storm sewer replacement or capital project, about $2.64 million per mile (City of Laramie, WY, consultant memo of 1 Dec 2023). Green: about $14,000 per curbside bioswale, installed (New Haven, CT, about 2023; see notes).
cost_quote: Improvements that require pipe replacement as well as implementation of the capital projects identified in the Master Plan have an average cost of approximately $500 per linear foot for storm sewers. If for example, the City provided a dedicated capital investment for one (1) mile of storm sewer replacement annually, the investment, at today’s prices, would be $2,640,000.
research_notes:
Philadelphia distance decay (same working paper): 'If we enlarge the treatment zone to 40m, the effect is at 5-6 percent of per square meter price; at 50 meters it goes further down to 3 percent.' The abstract says 'the causal impacts of GSI on single family residential sales prices per square foot of living area are in the range of 10 to 15 percent, on average.'

New Haven: Cohen, Dietz & Huang (2023), Lincoln Institute WP23JC1, https://storage.pardot.com/153411/16902983932kC1Snmu/Cohen_WP23JC1.pdf.
- Cost: 'Second, the New Haven Engineering Office has informed us that the full cost of a new bioswale similar to those currently installed in these neighborhoods, including installation costs and materials, is approximately $14,000.'
- Effect (executive summary): 'approximately an 8.8percent increase in residential property prices due to the presence of nearby bioswales in New Haven.'

effect:
Home values: none measured for snow clearing itself. The only related study (Dayton, Ohio hedonic regression) found that resident satisfaction with a bundle of city services that includes snow removal is positively related to sale prices; the abstract gives no size.

Safety: on Ontario highways during snowstorms, a 10% improvement in a road-surface condition index (the stand-in for plowing and salting) was associated with nearly an 11% reduction in expected collisions.

I found no study that measures how municipal sidewalk clearing changes pedestrian fall injuries.
effect_source: Usman, T., Fu, L., Miranda-Moreno, L.F. (2010). Accident Prediction Models for Quantifying Safety Benefit of Winter Road Maintenance. Transportation Research Board 89th Annual Meeting, paper 10-0774 (TRID record 909632). The journal version in Accident Analysis & Prevention 42(6), 2010, was not opened.
effect_quote: Among the main results, it was found that the RSI was statistically significant influencing the accident occurrence. According to our proposed index, our results suggest that a 10% improvement in road surface condition would lead to nearly an 11% reduction in the expected number of accidents.

name: Heated or enclosed bus shelters
trigger:
A GTFS stop (or parent station) with at least 16 scheduled bus departures between 07:00 and 09:00 on a representative weekday (8 or more an hour, from stop_times), where the nearest NOAA monthly normals station has a January MLY-TAVG-NORMAL (month=01) below 32°F.

Where stop boardings are available, Metro Transit's rule is a better filter: heat goes at major transfer points with at least 70 average daily boardings, and shelters at 20 or more daily boardings.

Caution: the Salt Lake City study found the shelter effect is larger at lower-frequency stops, where waits are longer.
trigger_data:
GTFS schedules for U.S. agencies listed in the Mobility Database Catalogs (MobilityData):
- Catalog CSV: https://files.mobilitydatabase.org/feeds_v2.csv (last modified 2026-11-06).
- README: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MobilityData/mobility-database-catalogs/main/README.md
- Terms: the catalog code is Apache 2.0. Each feed has its own optional license_url, and licenses vary by agency.

Climate: NOAA NCEI U.S. Monthly Climate Normals 1991-2020 (gov.noaa.ncdc:C01620, doi:10.25921/wck8-er13; revised 2023-05-15).
- Per-station CSV: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/normals-monthly/1991-2020/access/<STATION>.csv, field MLY-TAVG-NORMAL (°F).
- Free download; cite Palecki et al. (2021).
- More than 7,300 stations have temperature normals.
effect:
Home values: none measured.

Ridership (Salt Lake City, UTA stop-level data): extreme cold, extreme heat and heavy rain reduce ridership, and shelters have a 'modest' mitigating effect. The effect is larger on weekdays and at lower-frequency stops.

The authors' 2016 draft report (USDOT ROSA P) gives the sizes. On weekdays, an extreme-cold day (daily mean at or below the 10th percentile, about 26°F) lowered ridership at unsheltered stops by about 1.5% (log coefficient -0.0146; 7,300 stops). Shelters offset +0.00336, about a quarter of that loss (my arithmetic). There was no effect on weekends.

No study isolates heaters.
effect_source: Miao, Q., Welch, E.W., Sriraj, P.S. (2019). Extreme weather, public transport ridership and moderating effect of bus stop shelters. Journal of Transport Geography 74:125-133, doi:10.1016/j.jtrangeo.2018.11.007. I read the abstract on Arizona State University's research portal; ScienceDirect returned 403.
effect_quote: Using bus ridership data from the Salt Lake City metropolitan area, we find that extreme weather such as very high and low temperatures, and heavy rainfall reduces public transport ridership, while bus stop shelters have a modest effect on mitigating ridership losses resulting from these adverse weather conditions. The moderating effect of shelters is more pronounced on weekdays, and for bus stops with lower service frequency and fewer transfers.
cost:
Heated, lit BRT-station shelters: not to exceed $2,060,000 for 67 shelters, about $30,700 each (my arithmetic). That covers fabrication and delivery only; installation is in a separate construction contract (Metropolitan Council/Metro Transit, Minneapolis-St Paul, approved April 10, 2024).

Standard unheated three-wall shelter: $523,700 for 120 shelters, about $4,360 each. That is goods only; Metro Transit staff install them (January 2021).

This is a finished goods purchase for Duo-Gard Industries, Inc. to fabricate and deliver 67 shelters primarily for the E Line.

The report's text defines extreme cold as 'at or above 10th percentile (26 °F)', evidently a typo, since its tables use '<= 10th percentile'.

5. Wait-time perception (Fan, Guthrie & Levinson, CTS Report 16-01, Univ. of Minnesota, 2016; https://cts-d10resmod-prd.oit.umn.edu/pdf/cts-16-01.pdf): 'most waits at stops with no amenities are perceived at least 1.3 times as long as they actually are. name: Outdoor ice rink or sledding hill
trigger:
The nearest NOAA normals station has a January MLY-TAVG-NORMAL below 32°F, and no OpenStreetMap leisure=ice_rink (node or area, indoor or outdoor) lies within 5 km of the block group.

A better cold test for natural ice is DJF-TMAX-AVGNDS-LSTH032 ('Winter number of days with maximum temperature <= 32F') of 30 or more, because rinks need runs of freezing days. My count from the archive: 1,119 U.S. stations have a December-February mean below 32°F but fewer than 30 such days.
trigger_data:
OpenStreetMap leisure=ice_rink features (planet or Geofabrik extracts; updated continuously).
- License (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright): 'OpenStreetMap is open data, licensed under the Open Data Commons Open Database License (ODbL)'. Credit 'OpenStreetMap contributors'; derived databases must be shared under the same license.
- Tagging (https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Tag:leisure%3Dice_rink): skating lakes are tagged piste:type=ice_skate instead, and 'seasonal=yes should be used when it is only open in the cold season.'

Climate: NOAA NCEI Monthly Normals 1991-2020 (C01620, field MLY-TAVG-NORMAL) and Annual/Seasonal Normals (C01619, field DJF-TMAX-AVGNDS-LSTH032). Free download; cite Palecki et al. (2021).
effect:
None measured, for home values, health or use.

There is feasibility evidence only. The Minneapolis Park Board needs at least ten consecutive days below freezing, day and night, to establish ice. Canadian outdoor skating seasons shortened significantly at many stations between 1951 and 2005 (Damyanov et al. 2012).

effect_quote: It takes a minimum of ten consecutive days of below freezing temperatures during the day and night for ice to establish properly.

name: Weatherize and insulate older homes (program)
trigger:
All three must hold:
- The nearest NOAA normals station has ANN-HTDD-NORMAL (base 65°F) above 5,000, or a high ANN-CLDD-NORMAL for the 'very hot' branch.
- ACS 5-year B25034 shows more than half of housing units built before 1980.
- ACS B19013 block-group median household income is below the county median.

WAP eligibility itself is set per household: income at or below 200% of federal poverty guidelines, or 60% of state median income at the state's option. ACS C17002 (ratio of income to poverty level) would match that rule more closely. My count: 7,246 U.S. stations have HDD normals, and 4,108 exceed 5,000.
trigger_data:
NOAA NCEI Annual/Seasonal Normals 1991-2020 (gov.noaa.ncdc:C01619, doi:10.25921/4ek7-fk11), field ANN-HTDD-NORMAL ('Long-term averages of annual heating degree days with base 65F'). Free download; cite Palecki et al. (2021).

U.S. Census Bureau ACS 5-year tables B25034 (year structure built) and B19013 (median household income) for block groups, via the Census Data API (https://api.census.gov), released each December.
- Terms (https://www.census.gov/data/developers/about/terms-of-service.html): apps must display 'This product uses the Census Bureau Data API but is not endorsed or certified by the Census Bureau.' and must not re-identify people.
- My test query from this session got a 'Missing Key' page, so plan on a free API key.
effect:
Energy: in a randomized encouragement trial with about 30,000 eligible Michigan households, WAP cut monthly energy use by 10-20%, but upfront costs were about twice the realized savings. The published QJE version adds that model-projected savings were more than three times actual savings.

The DOE/ORNL national evaluation (program year 2008) found single-family homes saved $283 a year (12%): gas use fell 18% and electricity 7%. DOE now cites '$372 or more every year' (2022 dollars).

Home values: none measured for WAP-type retrofits. In a related study, Energy Star-certified homes sold for about 2% more in the Research Triangle and Portland, with no significant effect in Austin (Walls et al. 2017).
effect_source: Fowlie, M., Greenstone, M., Wolfram, C. (2015). Do Energy Efficiency Investments Deliver? Evidence from the Weatherization Assistance Program. NBER Working Paper 21331. Published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics 133(3):1597-1644 (2018); I read that abstract on RePEc because OUP returned 403.
effect_quote: We estimate that the WAP energy efficiency investments reduce monthly energy consumption by 10-20% on average. Although this surely provides a substantial assist to participating low-income households in the form of reduced energy bills, the upfront investment costs are about twice the realized energy savings.
cost:
DOE's program-year 2026 limit on the average cost per weatherized home is $8,813, covering labor, materials and related costs. It is the statutory $6,500 base adjusted by CPI (WPN 26-1, issued July 9, 2026).

Measured averages (DOE/ORNL summary, Aug 2015, and the Michigan study):
- PY2008: $4,695 total per home, of which $2,301 was DOE's share.
- PY2010: $6,812 total, of which $5,926 was DOE's share.
- Michigan study: $5,150 per household.
cost_quote: The percentage increase in the CPI for the previous 12-month period (January 2024–December 2024) was 3%. Therefore, the adjusted average expenditure limit for PY 2026 is $8,813.

name: Defensible space and home hardening (neighborhood program)
trigger: Block groups with homes that meet either test. (a) Nationwide: the share of the block group's land (suggested: block group plus a ~1 km buffer) in USFS Wildfire Hazard Potential 2023 class 4 (high) or 5 (very high) is at or above an engine threshold (suggested 10%). The buffer is needed because WHP codes developed land as 6 (non-burnable). (b) California: the engine's existing 'fire' share (block-group area in CAL FIRE Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zones, SRA 2023 / LRA 2025) is above 0. Optional refinement: the housing-weighted mean of WRC 2nd-edition Risk to Potential Structures (RPS) is in the top national tercile. The program is offered to a whole neighborhood because of the measured spillovers between neighbors.
trigger_data: USDA Forest Service, Wildfire Hazard Potential for the United States (270-m), version 2023, 4th ed. (Dillon 2023, RDS-2015-0047-4). Published 12/21/2023 and updated 07/17/2024. Covers CONUS, Alaska and Hawaii. Classified raster: 1 = very low, 2 = low, 3 = moderate, 4 = high, 5 = very high, 6 = non-burnable, 7 = water. County and ZIP summary tables are included. The data zip is 368 MB and downloads from www.fs.usda.gov (HTTP 200 checked 10 Nov 2026): https://www.fs.usda.gov/rds/archive/products/RDS-2015-0047-4/RDS-2015-0047-4_Data.zip (catalog page https://www.fs.usda.gov/rds/archive/catalog/RDS-2015-0047-4). Terms: 'These data were collected using funding from the U.S. Government and can be used without additional permissions or fees' (citation requested). Companion: Wildfire Risk to Communities, 2nd ed. (Scott et al. 2024, RDS-2020-0016-2, https://www.fs.usda.gov/rds/archive/catalog/RDS-2020-0016-2). It has 30 m rasters (RPS, burn probability, WHP and others) under the same terms. It spreads burn probability into developed areas, so it is better inside towns. But the files are very large and hosted on usfs-public.box.com (CONUS RPS 33.7 GB; California zip 11.1 GB); a ranged GET worked here. California only: the CAL FIRE FHSZ layers already used by the pipeline.
effect: Home values (California, sales 2013–2020, event-study difference-in-differences on home vintages): homes built after California's wildfire building codes took effect in high-hazard areas sell for 1.4%–2.5% more than homes built before the codes. The effect is on the home itself; the paper reports no distance-based effect. The author's benefit–cost check finds the premium roughly equals the cost of a basic set of wildfire fortifications. Losses avoided (Baylis & Boomhower, see notes): a 2008-or-newer California home is ~16 percentage points (40%) less likely to be destroyed when exposed (working paper; the published JPE estimate as cited by RFF is 13 points, or 34%). A code-built neighbor within 10 m lowers a home's destruction risk by ~2.5 points (6%). Caveat: the evidence is for code-built homes. No study measures the price effect of retrofits or defensible-space programs on existing homes.
effect_source: Wrenn, Douglas H. (2026). Wildfire risk and home prices: The case of California building codes. Journal of Housing Economics 72, article 102139 (June 2026), doi:10.1016/j.jhe.2026.102139. Crossref lists Wrenn as sole author. The abstract was read on Penn State's research portal because sciencedirect.com is not reachable from this session.
effect_quote: Using sales data from 2013–2020 in an event study difference-in-difference model of home vintages, we estimate that treated homes – those built after the codes went into effect – sell for 1.4%–2.5% more than homes built before the policies were enacted. Combining our estimates with home prices and estimates of costs to retrofit homes in a benefit–cost analysis reveals that premiums are roughly equal to the cost of meeting a basic set of wildfire fortifications.
cost: $52,408 average per completed home/site (construction $41,231 + defensible space $11,177). Source: California Wildfire Mitigation Program (Cal OES/CAL FIRE joint powers authority) pilot, 190 sites completed 2024 to 10 Sep 2026 in Lake, San Diego, Shasta and Siskiyou counties. County averages run from $35,543 (Siskiyou, mostly defensible space) to $71,875 (San Diego). The program pays the full cost ('upwards of $40,000') for households up to 120% of area median income. Above that, owners pay a 10% or 25% cost share.
cost_quote: To encourage broad neighborhood participation, the program covers the full cost of retrofit and defensible space implementation, upwards of $40,000, for homeowners earning up to 120 percent of the area median income. | Table '12. Cost Average Totals per Site' (columns Construction Total, Defensible Space Total, Grand Total): 'Total $41,230.85 $11,176.66 $52,407.51' — 'Shows the average total cost per home/site by county.'
research_notes: Losses avoided: Baylis & Boomhower, NBER WP 29621 (Dec 2021), https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w29621/w29621.pdf, published as JPE 134(3):895–948 (Mar 2026), doi:10.1086/739331. Quotes: 'A 2008 or newer home is about 16 percentage points (40%) less likely to be destroyed than a 1990 home experiencing an identical wildfire exposure.' and 'Our results imply that, all else equal, code-induced mitigation by a neighbor located less than 10 meters away (within the distance fire experts refer to as the home ignition zone) reduces a home’s likelihood of destruction during a wildfire by about 2.5 percentage points (6%).' The same WP: 'the costs of retrofitting existing homes to meet current wildfire building standards are substantial and our analysis suggest full retrofits are only economic in areas with extreme wildfire hazard.' RFF WP 25-30 (Ludington, Liao, Walls, Dec 2025; https://media.rff.org/documents/WP_25-30.pdf) cites the published version as finding homes 'are 13 percentage points less likely to be destroyed than similar homes built before the code was in effect (a 34 percent reduction from the sample mean of 39 percent).' Insurance discounts under California's Safer from Wildfires rule, from the same RFF WP (working_paper): 'Being in a Firewise USA community is valuable, providing an average discount of between $32 and $46, which is more than any single property-level action.' Also: 'Insurers that use the IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home program to set discounts provide an average discount of approximately $60 for the standard certification and $94 for the “Plus-level” certification.' And doing every property-level action gives 'a maximum discount of 5.65 percent, or approximately $98 for an average policy'. RFF concludes 'the costs of property retrofits are orders of magnitude greater than the insurance savings.' The rule itself, from a CDI release of 17 Oct 2022 (government, https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/2022/release076-2022.cfm): 'The regulation requires insurance companies to submit new rates that recognize the benefit of safety measures such as upgraded roofs and windows, defensible space, and community-wide programs such as Firewise USA and the Fire Risk Reduction Community designation developed by the state’s Board of Forestry and Fire Protection'. Other states' rules were not researched. Alternative cost estimate from a nonprofit (Headwaters Economics 2024, funded by CAL FIRE and the USDA Forest Service; https://headwaterseconomics.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/Wildfire_Retrofit_Report_20240624.pdf): 'for a typical 2,000-square-foot home in California, retrofitting costs can be as low as $2,000 for minimal retrofits to upwards of $100,000 if all retrofits to the highest level of protection are needed'. name: Water-wise landscaping and smart irrigation (turf-replacement rebates)
trigger: Block group where either test holds. (a) The NOAA 1991–2020 gridded annual precipitation normal (annprcp_norm), averaged over the block group, is under 20 in (508 mm). (b) The county had at least 50% of its area in D1 or worse (USDM 'cumulative' statistics, D1 column; suggested cut) in more than 25% of the weekly maps over the last 5 years (about 65 of 261 weeks). In both cases the block group must also be 'mostly lawns'. No national lawn layer was assessed; suggested proxy: ≥50% single-family detached homes (ACS B25024) or a high share of NLCD developed open-space and low-intensity land.
trigger_data: Drought: U.S. Drought Monitor county statistics, weekly maps since 2000, % of area in D0–D4 (cumulative or categorical). Downloads from https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/DmData/DataDownload.aspx or the API, e.g. https://usdmdataservices.unl.edu/api/CountyStatistics/GetDroughtSeverityStatisticsByAreaPercent?aoi=06037&startdate=1/1/2021&enddate=12/31/2025&statisticsType=1 (tested 10 Nov 2026; statisticsType=1 is cumulative, 2 is categorical). Terms (https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/About/Permission.aspx): 'The U.S. Drought Monitor map and associated data are available and authorized for use by third parties, including by commercial and non-commercial entities.' Credit must be given ('[Map / Data] courtesy of NDMC'). Rainfall: NOAA NCEI U.S. Monthly Gridded Climate Normals 1991–2020 (nClimGrid-based, 1/24° ≈ 4–5 km, contiguous U.S. only; annual normal variable annprcp_norm). File: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/oceans/archive/arc0196/0245564/1.1/data/0-data/prcp-1991_2020-monthly-normals-v1.0.nc (281 MB, Last-Modified 18 Jan 2022). Product page: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/us-climate-normals. Terms: federal NOAA data; NCEI's normals metadata says 'In most cases, electronic downloads of the data are free', with a no-warranty disclaimer. Alaska and Hawaii need station normals.
effect: Home values (Las Vegas valley, SNWA lawn-to-desert 'Cash-for-Grass' rebate participants, event studies and panel fixed effects): the average conversion raises the converted home's value by about 1%. There is little evidence of value spillovers to neighboring homes. The same conversions cut the home's water use by 19%–21% and may raise its energy use by 3%.
effect_source: Baker, Jonathan E. (2021). Subsidies for Succulents: Evaluating the Las Vegas Cash-for-Grass Rebate Program. Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists 8(3): 475–508, doi:10.1086/712429. The journal abstract was read on RePEc/IDEAS because journals.uchicago.edu is not reachable from this session.
effect_quote: Using event studies and panel fixed-effects models, I find that the average conversion reduces water use by 19%–21%, may increase energy use by 3%, and increases property values by about 1%. ... I find little evidence of property value spillovers to neighboring properties.
cost: $2.00 per sq ft of lawn replaced, up to 5,000 sq ft per year (Metropolitan Water District of Southern California base rebate via SoCal Water$mart, residential, page read 10 Nov 2026). Local agencies add to it. LADWP (Los Angeles) pays $5/sq ft in total ($3 LADWP + $2 MWD). SNWA (Las Vegas) pays $5.00/sq ft for the first 10,000 sq ft and $2.50/sq ft after that for single-family applicants as of 18 Sep 2025, but that rate may have ended (see notes). These are rebate (program) costs, not the full installed cost.
cost_quote: Metropolitan Water District is offering a rebate of $2.00 per square foot up to 5,000 square feet of converted yard per year. Your water agency may offer an additional rebate incentive.

name: Water recycling and secure water supply (regional project, local share)
trigger: Block groups whose HydroBASINS level-6 sub-basin(s), area-weighted, have a WRI Aqueduct 4.0 baseline annual water-stress category of 'High' (40–80%) or 'Extremely high' (>80%), or that are in a county meeting the USDM recurring-drought rule used for drought_landscaping. Model it as a utility/regional project: each block group carries a per-household local share of the regional cost (federal Title XVI grants can cover at most 25% in the 17 Western States).
trigger_data: WRI Aqueduct 4.0 Current and Future Global Maps Data, published 16 Aug 2023 (https://www.wri.org/data/aqueduct-global-maps-40-data). Global coverage by HydroBASINS level-6 sub-basin. Baseline water stress categories: Low <10%, Low-medium 10–20%, Medium-high 20–40%, High 40–80%, Extremely high >80%, plus 'Arid and low water use'. Zip of 261 MB with CSVs (Aqueduct40_baseline_annual_y2023m07d05.csv) and a file geodatabase: https://files.wri.org/aqueduct/aqueduct-4-0-water-risk-data.zip. License: the technical note (https://files.wri.org/d8/s3fs-public/2023-08/aqueduct-40-technical-note.pdf) says 'This work is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License'; the data page lists 'Creative Commons' without a version. Recurring drought: USDM county statistics (see drought_landscaping).
effect: Home values: none measured; searches found no U.S. hedonic study of recycled-water or supply-reliability projects. Losses avoided: across 53 California urban water utilities (more than 20 million customers), an annual supply disruption costs an average of $1,458 per acre-foot of shortage for a 10% shortage and $3,426 per acre-foot for a 30% shortage. Households would pay about $60–$600 a year to avoid an annual disruption, depending on shortage size and location.
effect_source: Buck, Steven; Auffhammer, Maximilian; Hamilton, Stephen; Sunding, David (2016). Measuring Welfare Losses from Urban Water Supply Disruptions. Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists 3(3): 743–778, doi:10.1086/687761. Abstract read on EconPapers; the journal site is not reachable from this session.
effect_quote: Welfare losses for an annual disruption range from an average of $1,458 per acre-foot of shortage for a 10% supply disruption to an average of $3,426 per acre-foot of shortage for a 30% supply disruption. cost: Indirect potable reuse in California, levelized, 2015 dollars: large projects (>12 million m3/yr) cost $0.91–$1.28 per m3, median $1.06/m3 (≈$1,120–$1,580 per acre-foot, median ≈$1,310/AF). The acre-foot figures are my conversions at 1,233.5 m3 per AF. The local share is the cost after federal and state grants, recovered through water rates.
cost_quote: The costs of small indirect potable reuse projects range from $1.21 to $1.80/m3, with a median cost of $1.50/m3. The cost of larger projects ranges from $0.91 to $1.28/m3, with a median cost of $1.06/m3.
cost_check: failed: The paper continues right after the quoted sentences: 'If the water is used to recharge groundwater prior to use, there is an additional cost of $0.37/m3 to convey the water to a groundwater basin, extract it from the aquifer, and treat it to drinking water standards. Thus, the total cost for small indirect potable reuse projects range from $1.59 to $2.17/m3 with a median cost of $1.88/m3. The total cost for large indirect potable reuse projects ranges from $1.28 to $1.66/m3, with a median cost of $1.43/m3.' My conversions at 1,233.5 m3/AF: large ≈ $1,580–$2,050/AF (median ≈ $1,760); small ≈ $1,960–$2,680/AF (median ≈ $2,320).

name: Cool or green roofs (rebates)
trigger: Block groups where the engine's heat measure ht is at least +1.1 °F, i.e. the Tree Equity Score block-group temp_diff (heat disparity) re-centred on the county's block-group mean (already computed by the pipeline). Optional extra condition: many low-rise roofs, e.g. a high single-family or low-rise share from ACS.
trigger_data: American Forests Tree Equity Score (block groups; per-state CSV zips used by the pipeline at https://tes-app-data-share.s3.amazonaws.com/<st>/<st>_csv.zip; e.g. az_csv.zip Last-Modified 27 Oct 2026; field temp_diff). Terms: no open data license found. The site copyright notice (https://www.treeequityscore.org/privacy) says American Forests 'expressly prohibits the copying of any protected or copyrighted materials' except fair use, and 'This prohibition includes the downloading of site content for commercial use or for use on personal websites'. Whether this covers the data downloads is unclear. Public-domain alternative for the same heat measure: USGS Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 Surface Temperature (Landsat 4–9, 1982–present; https://www.usgs.gov/landsat-missions/landsat-collection-2-surface-temperature). USGS policy: 'USGS-authored or produced data and information are considered to be in the U.S. Public Domain.'
effect: Home values: none measured. No hedonic study of cool (reflective) roofs was found, and a 2010 UC Berkeley literature review found none. Health (modelled, West Midlands, UK; summer 2006 and the 2003 and 2006 heatwaves): cool roofs across the whole city could offset 18% of seasonal heat deaths linked to the urban heat island (7% of all heat-related deaths), and about 25% of UHI-linked heat deaths during a heatwave. Energy (EPA summary of a modelling study): cool roofs can cut peak cooling demand 11–27% in air-conditioned homes.
effect_source: Macintyre, H.L.; Heaviside, C. (2019). Potential benefits of cool roofs in reducing heat-related mortality during heatwaves in a European city. Environment International 127: 430–441, doi:10.1016/j.envint.2019.02.065 (open-access copy on UCL Discovery).
effect_quote: Our results suggest that the UHI contributes up to 40% of heat related mortality over the summer period and that cool roofs implemented across the whole city could potentially offset 18% of seasonal heat-related mortality associated with the UHI (corresponding to 7% of total heat-related mortality).
cost: Rebate of up to $0.60 per sq ft of qualifying cool roof (LADWP Consumer Rebate Program, Los Angeles, 2024 fact sheet). Installed cost, from US EPA's 2008 compendium citing a 2006 report: cool coatings on low-slope roofs cost $0.75–$1.50/sq ft for materials and labor; single-ply membranes cost $1.50–$3.00/sq ft. For most products the premium over conventional roofing is $0 to $0.05–0.10/sq ft. Green roofs start at $10/sq ft for extensive roofs and $25/sq ft for intensive roofs (EPA, citing a 2001 report). The installed costs are old (see notes).
cost_quote: Cool Roofs: up to $0.60 per square feet
research_notes: EPA Compendium, Cool Roofs chapter (https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2017-05/documents/reducing_urban_heat_islands_ch_4.pdf): 'Cool roof coatings might cost between $0.75 and $1.50 per square foot for materials and labor, which includes routine surface preparation like pressure-washing, but which does not include repair of leaks, cracks, or bubbling of the existing roof surface.' and 'In terms of dollars per square foot, the premium ranges from zero to 5 or 10 cents for most products'. EPA Green Roofs chapter (https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2017-05/documents/reducing_urban_heat_islands_ch_3.pdf): 'A 2001 report estimated that initial costs start at $10 per square foot (0.09 m2) for the simpler, extensive roof and $25 per square foot for intensive roofs.' EPA cool roofs page (https://www.epa.gov/heatislands/using-cool-roofs-reduce-heat-islands): 'In air-conditioned residential buildings, solar reflectance from a cool roof can reduce peak cooling demand by 11–27%.' This rests on a modelling study (Synnefa et al. 2007). U.S. modelling for Los Angeles (Kalkstein et al. 2022, Int J Biometeorol 66:911–925, https://escholarship.org/content/qt08v664xk/qt08v664xk.pdf) combines more trees with higher-albedo roofs and pavement: 'We found that roughly one in four lives currently lost during heat waves could be saved.' That result is not roof-only. No measured home-value effect, per the CREC review (Kroll & Cray 2010, UC Berkeley, https://uc-ciee.org/ciee-old/downloads/CRECHedonicAnalysis.pdf): 'our queries identified no hedonic property valuation articles addressing roof characteristics and only seven articles addressing pavement, none of which focused on pavement attributes relevant to cool community design.' The often-cited green-roof rent premium (Ichihara & Cohen 2011, Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences 4(1):21–30, doi:10.1007/s12076-010-0046-4) could not be opened and is not used. The catalog already has cool_pavement and cooling_center types on the same ht ≥ 1.1 trigger.

name: Community storm shelter or safe rooms
trigger: The block group sits in a census tract whose FEMA National Risk Index tornado rating (TRND_RISKR) is 'Relatively High' or 'Very High'. In NRI v1.20 (Dec 2025) that is 21,559 of 85,154 tracts: 15,946 Relatively High plus 5,613 Very High (my count from the FEMA feature service). Rank block groups higher where mobile homes are common, measured as ACS 2020-2024 B25024_010E / B25024_001E. Nationally 5.6% of housing units are mobile homes. Of the 239,637 block groups that have housing, 17.9% are at or above 10% mobile homes and 10.5% are at or above 20% (my computation from the 2020-2024 table-based summary file). The reason for ranking this way: shelters cost about 11 times less per life saved in mobile homes than in permanent homes. FEMA P-361 says to site the shelter within a 1/4-mile walk or 1/2-mile drive of the homes it serves. For local display only, the SPC (E)F2+ tornado paths since 1950 can be shown: 13,404 of 73,458 tracks, which account for 6,061 of 6,341 deaths (my count from the SPC CSV).
trigger_data: (1) FEMA National Risk Index, 'National Risk Index Census Tracts' feature service, field TRND_RISKR (Tornado - Hazard Type Risk Index Rating). Its values are Very High, Relatively High, Relatively Moderate, Relatively Low, Very Low, No Rating and Insufficient Data. Version December 2025 (1.20.0); item modified 18 Dec 2025. Service: https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Census_Tracts/FeatureServer/0. Item page: https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=9da4eeb936544335a6db0cd7a8448a51. Covers all census tracts nationwide. FEMA NRI terms: use is free, but you must cite the dataset, its version and the access date, and state that the product 'uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's National Risk Index dataset API or downloadable datasets but is not endorsed by FEMA'. Reverse engineering is not allowed; the data are for planning only. (2) ACS 2020-2024 5-year table B25024, Units in Structure (B25024_010E 'Mobile home'; B25024_001E total), at block-group level: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b25024.dat. Variable list: https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5/groups/B25024.json. The summary file needs no key. Census API terms require the notice 'This product uses the Census Bureau Data API but is not endorsed or certified by the Census Bureau.' (3) NOAA/NWS Storm Prediction Center SVRGIS tornado paths 1950-2025, page updated 23 April 2026: https://www.spc.noaa.gov/gis/svrgis/zipped/1950-2025-torn-aspath.zip. CSV of single tracks: https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/data/1950-2025_actual_tornadoes.csv (fields include mag, fat, inj, slat, slon, elat, elon, len, wid). The data are lines and points, public domain per https://www.weather.gov/disclaimer.
effect: Home values: none measured. No study was found on how a community shelter affects nearby home values. The closest housing-market evidence is from Oklahoma manufactured-home parks: lot rents in parks with shelters were 5-8% higher, which is about enough to pay for the shelters. That estimate is statistically significant in only one specification (Simmons & Sutter 2007). Safety and cost-effectiveness: in Oklahoma, at a 3% real discount rate, a shelter costs about $6.0 million per life saved in mobile homes against $68 million in permanent homes. By that measure, shelters are cost-effective for mobile homes in the most tornado-prone states but not for permanent homes (Simmons & Sutter 2006, Risk Analysis).
effect_source: Kevin Simmons and Daniel Sutter (2007), 'Tornado shelters and the manufactured home parks market', Natural Hazards 43(3): 365-378, doi:10.1007/s11069-007-9123-4. The abstract was read on IDEAS/RePEc because the Springer page returned a bot check.
effect_quote: We find that rents for lots in parks with shelters are 5–8% higher, which generates sufficient revenue to approximately pay for shelters, but the point estimate is statistically significant in only one specification.
cost: One project: $1,657,000 total construction cost for a 10,000 sq ft, FEMA P-361 multi-purpose safe room for 1,592 people at Coahoma Community College in Clarksdale, Mississippi. FEMA HMGP paid 90% ($1,491,300); the award was announced in Sept 2016. That works out to about $166 per sq ft and about $1,040 per occupant (my arithmetic). A second check: three Missouri school safe rooms approved in March 2019 imply about $1,700-$2,000 per occupant, total cost. I derived this from the federal shares, match rates and capacities in the SEMA release.
cost_quote: Federal funding, which totals $1,491,300, represents 90 percent of the $1,657,000 total construction cost.
research_notes:
Size and capacity of the cost example, from the same page: "The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Hazard Mitigation Grant Program award will support construction of a 10,000-square-foot safe room built to FEMA-361 standards to protect people during hurricane or tornado-force winds." and "When completed, the safe room will be able to protect 1,592 students, faculty, staff, and residents within a half-mile radius of Coahoma Community College."

Missouri SEMA release, 7 Mar 2019 (https://sema.dps.mo.gov/news/newsitem/uuid/63c958e8-db88-4210-91d3-febc28703e32): "The federal share of the Sparta project is approximately $1.4 million. The federal share of the Neosho project is approximately $1.1 million, and the federal share for the Miller project is approximately $925,000." Capacities are 1,089 (Sparta), 660 (Goodman/Neosho) and 519 (Miller). The local match is 25% for Sparta and 10% for the other two. That gives totals of about $1.87M, $1.22M and $1.03M, or $1,714, $1,852 and $1,980 per occupant (my arithmetic). On funding, the same release says: "The FEMA Pre-Disaster Mitigation grant program provides 75 percent funding for approved safe room projects, which rises to 90 percent for communities meeting small size and low income levels."

FEMA P-361, 4th ed., April 2021, read on a Texas state mirror because fema.gov returned 403 (https://newtools.cira.state.tx.us/upload/page/12213/docs/SR/FEMA%20Publication%20P-361.pdf). On funding: "As of November 2020, FEMA has provided approximately $1.2 billion in FEMA funds towards the design and construction of over 40,000 residential and nearly 2,200 community safe rooms in 25 states and territories." On sizing: "Tornado safe rooms: ICC 500 Section 502.2 requires a minimum of 5 square feet per person for standing or seated occupants for community tornado safe rooms." On service area: "indicates a ¼-mile radius for occupants walking to the safe room; a ½-mile travel distance typically applies to occupants driving to a community safe room." P-361 (2021) describes cost increases only qualitatively. Its benefit-cost tool takes tornado probability from NOAA records.

Safety evidence. Simmons & Sutter 2006, Risk Analysis 26(4): 945-954 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/wly/riskan/v26y2006i4p945-954.html): "Despite the very different method used, the estimates are $68 million in permanent homes and $6.0 in mobile homes in Oklahoma using a 3% real discount rate, within about 10% of estimates based on historical fatalities. The findings suggest that shelters provide cost-effective protection for mobile homes in the most tornado-prone states but not for permanent homes." The Natural Hazards abstract (effect_url) says: "In the US over 40% of tornado fatalities occur in mobile homes even though they comprise about 8% of US housing units." Simmons & Sutter 2008, Weather and Forecasting 23(2): 246-258 (https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/wefo/23/2/2007waf2006027_1.xml): "If mobile homes compose an additional 1% of a county’s housing stock, expected fatalities increase by about 6.6%." The CDC study of the April 2011 Alabama tornadoes (PLOS ONE, see warning_sirens): "Mobile home residents showed the highest odds of injury (OR, 6.98; 95% CI: 2.10–23.20). No severe injuries occurred in tornado shelters."

NIBS, Natural Hazard Mitigation Saves 2019 (https://nibs.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/NIBS_MMC_MitigationSaves_2019-1.pdf), on a sample of FEMA-funded wind grants: "Large facilities with dual purposes, such as school gymnasia and cafeterias, exhibit an average BCR of 8.0."

I found no nationwide public list of existing community safe rooms, so 'no shelter nearby' cannot be tested. Keep kind 'qol', since no effect on nearby home values has been measured.

name: Outdoor warning sirens and alerts

Basis for 1.5 km: Clinton County (Ohio) EMA says a siren may be heard about a mile away on a calm day, but less than half a mile away upwind during storms. Texas TWDB defines a siren's coverage as the area that receives at least 70 dB. Show this as 'no siren mapped', not 'no siren', because OSM mapping is incomplete. In Nov 2026 Geofabrik extracts, St. Charles County, MO had 135 mapped sirens against the 143 the county reports. Sedgwick County, KS had only 87 against the 153 the county maintains (my count inside TIGERweb county polygons).
trigger_data: (1) OpenStreetMap features tagged emergency=siren. Tag definition: https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Tag:emergency%3Dsiren (optional siren:purpose=tornado, siren:range). Get them from Geofabrik state extracts or Overpass. Taginfo counts 26,178 tagged objects worldwide, data until 2026-11-09 (https://taginfo.openstreetmap.org/api/4/tag/stats?key=emergency&value=siren). The data are points and are updated continuously. License: ODbL (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright): free to copy and adapt with credit to OpenStreetMap and its contributors; share-alike. Coverage is uneven. My counts in the project's Nov 2026 state extracts: Iowa 2,262, Missouri 488, Oklahoma 369, Kansas 159, Alabama 74. (2) FEMA NRI tract field TRND_RISKR, v1.20 (Dec 2025): https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Census_Tracts/FeatureServer/0. FEMA NRI terms require a citation and a non-endorsement statement. (3) NOAA SPC tornado paths 1950-2025, for display: https://www.spc.noaa.gov/gis/svrgis/ (public domain).
effect: Home values: none measured; I found no study of sirens and home prices. Safety: CDC ran a case-control study of the 27 April 2011 Alabama tornadoes with 98 injured cases and 200 uninjured controls. People who received the siren warning had half the odds of injury (adjusted odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.30-0.85), and people who heard sirens more often had lower odds of injury. No study was found that links a community's siren coverage to tornado deaths. For warnings in general, Simmons & Sutter (2008) found injuries fell by over 40% at some lead times, while results for deaths were mixed.
effect_source: Thomas Niederkrotenthaler, Erin M. Parker, Fernando Ovalle, Rebecca E. Noe, Jeneita Bell, Likang Xu, Melissa A. Morrison, Caitlin E. Mertzlufft and David E. Sugerman (2013), 'Injuries and Post-Traumatic Stress following Historic Tornados: Alabama, April 2011', PLOS ONE 8(12): e83038, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0083038.
effect_quote: Exposure to warnings via the Internet (aOR, 0.20; 95% CI: 0.09–0.49), television (aOR, 0.45; 95% CI: 0.24–0.83), and sirens (aOR, 0.50; 95% CI: 0.30–0.85) decreased the odds of injury, and residents frequently exposed to tornado sirens had lower odds of injury.
cost: $30,000-$50,000 to install one outdoor warning siren (St. Charles County, Missouri, county page current as of 2026). A Texas Water Development Board guide (Jan 2026, based on 2025 interviews) gives $24,000-$70,000 per siren for capital and installation. It puts maintenance at about 10% of installation cost per year. Ann Arbor expects about $17,000 a year to maintain its 22 sirens, about $770 per siren (my arithmetic).
cost_quote: The cost of installing a siren now ranges between $30,000 and $50,000.
research_notes:

It says installation can push this to $40-50K. On range: "On a calm day, you might hear a siren from a mile away." and "If you’re standing in an upwind direction, you may not hear the siren even from less than half a mile away."

name: Residential safe room rebates
trigger: The block group sits in a census tract with NRI TRND_RISKR 'Relatively High' or 'Very High', and many of its homes are owner-occupied houses that can take an in-home or in-ground safe room. Measure this with the ACS 2020-2024 shares of B25024_002E ('1, detached') and B25003_002E ('Owner occupied'). Block groups with many mobile homes are better served by storm_shelter.
trigger_data: (1) FEMA NRI tract field TRND_RISKR, v1.20 (Dec 2025): https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Census_Tracts/FeatureServer/0. FEMA NRI terms require a citation, the version and access date, and a non-endorsement statement. (2) ACS 2020-2024 5-year tables at block-group level: B25024, Units in Structure (https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b25024.dat), and B25003, Tenure (https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b25003.dat). Variable labels were checked at api.census.gov. The Census API terms notice applies. (3) NOAA SPC tornado paths 1950-2025, for display: https://www.spc.noaa.gov/gis/svrgis/ (public domain per https://www.weather.gov/disclaimer).
effect: Oklahoma City homes with a tornado shelter sold for 3.5% to 4% more, about $4,200 at the 2005 mean sale price. At the time, shelters cost $2,500-$3,000 installed (Simmons & Sutter 2007). This premium applies only to the house that has the shelter; no effect on neighbors was measured. Safety per dollar is low in permanent homes: about $30 million per life saved without discounting (Merrell, Simmons & Sutter 2005), or $68 million at a 3% discount rate (Simmons & Sutter 2006).
effect_source: Kevin Simmons and Daniel Sutter (2007), 'Tornado shelters and the housing market', Construction Management and Economics 25(11): 1119-1126, doi:10.1080/01446190701618299. The abstract was read on IDEAS/RePEc because the Taylor & Francis page returned 403.
effect_quote: We find that a shelter increases the sale price of a home by 3.5% to 4% or approximately $4200 given the mean price of homes sold in 2005. The magnitude of the premium is plausible given that shelters retail for $2500-$3000 installed.
cost: For a safe room built during construction of a new home: $9,400-$13,100 for 8 x 8 ft and $18,900-$25,500 for 14 x 14 ft (FEMA P-320, 5th ed., March 2021; 2019 dollars, national RSMeans averages, 15% contingency). A tested door adds about $2,500-$3,200. Retrofits cost more. Small steel in-ground units cost $5,000-$6,000 before installation and delivery. As a rebate example, Michigan's FEMA-funded program pays 75% of the cost, up to $7,131.75.
cost_quote: During the construction of a new home, the estimated basic cost to construct a safe room using the design plans in this publication ranges from approximately $9,400 to $13,100 for an 8-foot × 8-foot safe room and from $18,900 to $25,500 for a 14-foot × 14-foot safe room
research_notes:
This type was added by the research step; it was not on the mapping list. The group brief names residential safe rooms, and the only measured home-value effect in this group is for a house with its own shelter. Fold it into storm_shelter if one type is preferred. Because a home-value effect is measured, it could be a 'value' type.

The P-320 PDF is FEMA's March 2021 edition, read on a Texas state mirror because fema.gov returned 403. FEMA's 6th edition (Dec 2024) could not be opened. From the same PDF: "Estimates of safe room designs for each construction type were developed using industry-accepted cost-estimating guides and are provided in 2019 dollars." On doors: "Market research shows that entry level prices for properly tested and labeled residential safe room door assemblies are between approximately $2,500 and $3,200 at the time of this publication." On retrofits: "Further, safe rooms installed in existing homes will be more expensive than those built as part of new construction." On prefabricated units: "Small steel in-ground units typically cost between $5,000 and $6,000 not including installation (excavation and ground anchors) and delivery fee." P-320 also repeats the roughly 3.5% / $4,200 price premium.

Rebate program example: the Michigan State Police EMHSD Safe Room Rebate Program FAQ (BRIC-funded; https://www.michigan.gov/msp/divisions/emhsd/response-recovery-responsive/michigan-safe-room-rebate-program/faqs): "Homeowners who are selected for the program are eligible for a rebate of 75% of the eligible cost to install/construct a safe room up to a maximum of $7,131.75. This amount is 75% of the predetermined benefit amount for safe rooms of $9,509."

P-361 (2021) reports over 40,000 FEMA-funded residential safe rooms as of Nov 2020.

name: Land bank takes tax-delinquent and nuisance properties
trigger: pop2020 < pop2010 (Decennial P1_001N; re-tabulate 2010 block-group counts to 2020 block groups with the Census relationship file) AND other_vacant_share = ACS B25004_008E / B25001_001E >= 0.10 (2020-2024 ACS 5-year; my proposal: the mapping step's 0.05 flags 30.2% of US block groups with 50+ housing units in my own tabulation, while 0.10 flags 14.7%) AND the state is one of the 20 states plus Puerto Rico with a land-bank enabling law, or a land bank or land-banking program already serves the county (Center for Community Progress map). Optional value screen: ACS B25077 median value so low that land is worth less than acquisition plus demolition.
trigger_data: (1) U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 2020-2024 5-year, table B25004 Vacancy Status (line 008 'Other vacant') and B25001 Housing Units, by block group. Table-based summary file https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b25004.dat (file dated 29 Jan 2026; 242,297 block-group rows) or the Census Data API, which now needs a free key (keyless requests redirect to missing_key.html). Public Census data under census.gov policies and the API Terms of Service. (2) 2010 and 2020 Census P.L. 94-171 counts (P1 population, H1 housing units) by block group, plus the 2020-to-2010 block group relationship file https://www2.census.gov/geo/docs/maps-data/data/rel2020/blkgrp/tab20_blkgrp20_blkgrp10_natl.txt (public). (3) Center for Community Progress National Land Bank Map https://communityprogress.org/resources/land-banks/national-land-bank-map/: land bank point locations, 'updated as of May 2026', with 20 states plus Puerto Rico holding enabling laws as of June 2026. The site says '© 2026 All Rights Reserved', so use it as a lookup or link, not as open data. HUD-USPS vacancy data cannot be used for a public map (see notes).
effect: Cuyahoga County (Cleveland), OH, home sales 2009-2013. In the six months before the land bank buys it, each distressed property within 500 ft lowers a home's sale price by 5.2%. Once the land bank owns it the discount falls to 4.4%, a gain of 0.8 percentage points per property within 500 ft; this gap is not always statistically significant. After a land-bank demolition the vacant lot's discount is 2.4%. Estimated value preserved: about $3.8M for homes sold during the 39-month study and about $156M for homes that did not sell.
effect_source: Whitaker, S. and Fitzpatrick IV, T.J. (2014). Land Bank 2.0: An Empirical Evaluation. Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland Working Paper 12-30R (Sept 2014). Published as Journal of Regional Science 56(1):156-175 (2016), confirmed on IDEAS.
effect_quote: In the six months before they are purchased by the land bank, the distressed properties are estimated to lower the sale price of nearby homes (within 500 feet) by 5.2 percent. The preferred model suggests that a land bank acquisition reduces the distressed property’s negative externality by 0.8 percentage points from 5.2 percent to 4.4 percent.

Fifteen years ago, Frangos spearheaded the establishment of the Cuyahoga Land Bank, Ohio’s first county land bank, which has since transacted over 14,000 properties and played a critical role in Cuyahoga County’s revitalization.

name: Side-lot program (vacant lots sold to next-door owners)
trigger: pop2020 < pop2010 AND housing units fell 2010-2020 (Decennial H1_001N). A fall in units signals demolitions that left vacant lots; this is my inference. Also require owner-occupied homes nearby (ACS B25003_002E share of occupied units, e.g. >= 30%; my proposal), because side lots go to the occupied home next door. Where a local assessor or land-bank parcel file exists, count publicly held vacant residential lots that share a side or rear line with an owner-occupied parcel.
trigger_data: (1) 2010 and 2020 Census P.L. 94-171 P1 and H1 by block group, with the 2020-to-2010 block group relationship file https://www2.census.gov/geo/docs/maps-data/data/rel2020/blkgrp/tab20_blkgrp20_blkgrp10_natl.txt (public). (2) ACS 2020-2024 5-year B25003 Tenure by block group (table-based summary file, released Jan 2026; public, API key needed). (3) No national public dataset of vacant residential parcels exists; parcel aggregators are proprietary. HUD notes that 'In distressed areas, a reduction in total AMS addresses from quarter-to-quarter appears to be a strong indicator of where demolition is occurring.' (https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/usps.html). However, those tract-level USPS data are restricted to registered government and nonprofit users and cannot be redistributed.
