name: Strategic demolition of vacant, unsalvageable homes
trigger: pop2020 < pop2010 AND other_vacant_share (B25004_008E / B25001_001E) >= 0.10; the strong case is >= 0.20, which covers 3.7% of US block groups (own tabulation, ACS 2020-2024). Also require ACS B25077 median value at the bottom of the metro range, so that land value does not cover acquisition plus demolition. Prefer moderate over extreme blight: in Detroit, value gains appeared only where blight was low before demolition, and firearm-assault reductions were larger with 6-12 demolitions per block group than with 13 or more.
trigger_data: (1) ACS 2020-2024 5-year B25004, B25001 and B25077 by block group (www2.census.gov table-based summary files dated Jan 2026; Census API needs a key; public). (2) 2010 and 2020 P.L. 94-171 P1 and H1 by block group, with the relationship file https://www2.census.gov/geo/docs/maps-data/data/rel2020/blkgrp/tab20_blkgrp20_blkgrp10_natl.txt. (3) HUD-USPS vacancy durations by tract, quarterly (https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/usps.html). HUD defines vacant addresses as those 'identified as being vacant (not collecting their mail) for 90 days or longer'. These data are restricted to registered governmental and nonprofit users and the sublicense bars distribution, so use them internally at most.
effect: Cleveland (Cuyahoga Land Bank, sales 2009-2013): demolishing a distressed house cuts its drag on homes within 500 ft from -5.2% to -2.4%, a gain of 2.8 percentage points. That gap is not statistically significant in the preferred model (p=0.18); other models give 1.4 to 4.1 points. Detroit (Hardest Hit Fund demolition program from 2014, sales 2009-2019): no average effect on prices, and a modest positive effect only where blight was low beforehand (Alvayay Torrejón et al. 2023). Lee et al. (2025) found 'consistently lower values near Demolition sites'. Safety: Detroit block groups with more than 5 demolitions had 11% fewer firearm assaults (95% CI 7-15%) (Jay et al. 2019).
effect_source: Whitaker, S. and Fitzpatrick IV, T.J. (2014). Land Bank 2.0: An Empirical Evaluation. Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland WP 12-30R; Journal of Regional Science 56(1):156-175 (2016).
effect_quote: By demolishing a distressed property the Land Bank reduces its impact 2.8 percentage points from 5.2 to 2.4. The tract fixed effect model suggests no value is recovered by acquisition and 1.4 percentage points is recovered by demolition.
effect_check: failed: Replace 'home sales 2009-2013' with 'single-family home sales January 2010 - March 2013 (44,375 sales, 39 months)'. Source text: 'Out of the 44,375 sales between January 2010 and March 2013'. In effect_quote, put '...' between the two sentences. | Replace 'Cleveland (Cuyahoga Land Bank, sales 2009-2013)' with 'Cleveland (Cuyahoga Land Bank, single-family sales January 2010 - March 2013)'. Source text: 'Out of the 44,375 sales between January 2010 and March 2013'.
cost: $14,100 to $17,643 per house (Michigan, demolitions funded by the TARP Hardest Hit Fund). The average rose from $9,266 to $17,643 per house in under three years up to mid-2016, then fell to about $14,100 in the first half of FY2017. Detroit averaged $17,622 at the June 2016 audit. Ohio rose from $9,293 to $15,019 per house. Detroit's whole program demolished over 20,800 properties for over $250 million, about $12,000 each (derived).
cost_quote: In Michigan, which accounts for nearly half of all committed TARP dollars, the average cost of demolition paid with TARP dollars increased by 90% in less than three years from $9,266 per house to $17,643. In Ohio, the average cost of demolitions charged to TARP increased 62% over 2 ½ years (from $9,293 per house to $15,019).
research_notes: Mapping-step type; overlaps the existing blight_rehab type ('Rehab or replace blighted homes'). Detroit, the program named in the ask: Alvayay Torrejón, Paredes & Skidmore (2023), Journal of Regional Science 63(5):1073-1099 (abstract at https://econpapers.repec.org/article/blajregsc/v_3a63_3ay_3a2023_3ai_3a5_3ap_3a1073-1099.htm): 'On average, blight removal through the demolition program does not appear to have been capitalized into the residential property prices. However, when considering the effect of ex‐ante program property characteristics, we find a modest positive effect of demolitions on property prices in areas with a low level of blight before the demolitions.' The same abstract says the program 'has demolished more than 20,800 properties at the cost of over $250 million'. Paredes & Skidmore (2016 working paper; Regional Science and Urban Economics 66:16-27, 2017), https://ideas.repec.org/p/cat/dtecon/dt201607.html: 'Using efficiency as the criteria for justifying spending public funds on demolition, average property values would have to increase by a factor of five to justify the demolition program.' Safety: Jay et al. (2019), J Behav Med 42(4):626-634, PMID 31367928 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31367928/): 'Receiving over 5 demolitions was associated with a 11% reduction in firearm assaults, relative to comparable control locations, 95% CI [7%, 15%], p = 0.01.' It found no effect on drug crime and no displacement. Cleveland: 'The difference between the coefficients (2.8) does not reach statistical significance (p=0.18).' name: Urban farm or forest on assembled vacant land
trigger: pop2020 < pop2010 AND enough cleared land in the block group or an adjacent one to assemble at least 0.5 acre for a farm or 10,000 sq ft for a forest patch (Baltimore and USDA Forest Service siting criteria). Nationwide proxy: housing units lost 2010-2020 (Decennial H1_001N) in the block group plus its neighbors, treating each lost unit as roughly one cleared lot (my inference; lot sizes vary), AND a high other_vacant_share. Confirm with local parcel or land-bank inventories.
trigger_data: (1) 2010 and 2020 Census P.L. 94-171 P1 and H1 by block group, with the relationship file https://www2.census.gov/geo/docs/maps-data/data/rel2020/blkgrp/tab20_blkgrp20_blkgrp10_natl.txt (public). (2) ACS 2020-2024 B25004 and B25001 by block group (Jan 2026). (3) There is no national open vacant-land or parcel dataset; local assessor files are needed to confirm that assemblable acreage exists.
effect: Home values: none measured for urban farms or planted forests on assembled vacant land; no study was found, and Detroit's Hantz Woodlands is unstudied. Safety, from Youngstown, OH, a shrinking city where 23,831 of 62,569 parcels were vacant in 2010: under the 'Lots of Green' program, vacant lots converted to community reuse (mostly community gardens and orchards) saw significant drops in felony assaults and burglaries compared with matched untreated lots. Motor-vehicle thefts rose. The nearest home-value analog is New York City community gardens, which raised neighboring values 'especially in the poorest neighborhoods' (Voicu & Been 2008); that evidence belongs to the existing community_garden type.
effect_source: Kondo, M., Hohl, B., Han, S., Branas, C. (2016). Effects of greening and community reuse of vacant lots on crime. Urban Studies 53(15):3279-3295 (author copy via USDA Forest Service Treesearch, PDF https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/49785.pdf).
effect_quote: Regression models adjusted for spatial autocorrelation found the most consistent significant reductions in burglaries around stabilisation lots, and in assaults around community reuse lots. Spill-over crime reduction effects were found in contiguous areas around newly treated lots.
cost: About $60,000 per acre to set up a commercial urban farm on city-owned vacant land (derived). Strength to Love Farm, Sandtown-Winchester, Baltimore, broke ground June 2013: 1.5 acres, $90,000 in site costs covering site acquisition, preparation and permits, hoop houses and growing media, equipment, and utility hookups. Farming labor and operating costs are excluded.
cost_quote: The 1.5-acre site is being leased from HCD as part of “Homegrown Baltimore”, a program to increase healthy food access in the City, especially in neighborhoods lacking grocery stores. ... Site Costs = $90,000 ... Farming labor, insurance, production costs, tools, marketing, etc., not included.
research_notes: Mapping-step type. The cost source is USDA Forest Service NRS-INF-32-15 (Sept 2015), 'Green Pattern Book', written with the City of Baltimore and read from EPA's archived copy. Siting criteria from the same book: 'Sites for urban agriculture should be a minimum 1/2 acre lot (or collection of lots).' and 'Minimum size of 10,000 square feet for forest patches; smaller areas might be used for buffers'. Youngstown magnitudes for all greening treatments combined (GLS, authors' log-point reading): '85% reduction in felony assaults, 24% reduction in burglaries, 69% reduction in robberies, and 7% reduction in thefts, and 53% increase in motor vehicle thefts holding all other values constant.' Voicu & Been (2008), Real Estate Economics 36(2):241-283 (abstract at https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/reesec/v36y2008i2p241-283.html): 'We find that gardens have significant positive effects, especially in the poorest neighborhoods. Higher‐quality gardens have the greatest positive impact.' I did not verify its magnitudes. Lighter tree and green-infrastructure lot treatments in Detroit (The Greening of Detroit, funded by DWSD, 2013, 10 lots, mostly volunteer labor; nonprofit document https://detroitfuturecity.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/02/Vacant-Land-Treatment-Program.pdf): 'The cost per lot is $2,500, with a total estimated cost of $25,000.' Tri-COG (Allegheny County) found green-infrastructure lots had 'a more positive effect than blighted vacant lots' but no conclusive estimate by submarket. Tiny forests and community gardens already exist as catalog types.

name: Replace lead water service lines
trigger: The block group falls inside the service area of a public water system (EPA boundaries, joined on PWSID) whose inventory under the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions reports lead or galvanized-requiring-replacement (GRR) service lines, or many lines of unknown material, in EPA's SDWIS Service Line Inventory. Rank by the system's lead-line count per service connection times the share of homes built before 1980 (ACS B25034). Not limited to shrinking cities, but lead lines cluster in older industrial cities.
trigger_data: (1) EPA SDWIS Federal Reporting Services, Service Line Inventory https://sdwis.epa.gov/ords/sfdw_pub/r/sfdw/sdwis_fed_reports_public/service-line-inventory: counts of lead, GRR, non-lead and unknown lines for each public water system, from state submissions; the filter lists quarters 2025Q1 through 2026Q3. Public EPA data. (2) EPA Public Water System Service Area Boundaries v3 (March 2026) https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/public-water-system-service-areas: over 44,000 community water systems covering about 99% of the population they serve, linked by PWSID. Mixes modeled and state-sourced boundaries; EPA 'disclaims responsibility for the spatial accuracy and attribution of these GIS features'. (3) ACS 2020-2024 B25034 Year Structure Built by block group (public).
effect: Rhode Island (Providence Water service area): replacing the public-side lead line raised home sale prices 7-8%, about $16,000-$19,000 on the $238,000 average sale. It also cut children's blood lead by about 0.4 µg/dL. Information alone had little effect: after DC Water published its lead-line map in 2016, prices of homes with and without lead lines did not diverge significantly (Jiang 2022).
effect_source: Marcus, M. (2023). Burying the Lead: Effects of Public Lead Service Line Replacements on Blood Lead Levels and Property Values. Vanderbilt University and NBER working paper, NBER conference version dated July 22, 2023.
effect_quote: Replacements significantly reduced child blood lead levels by about 0.4 µg/dL, increased property values by 7-8 percent, and increased the probability of moving among renters.
cost: $6,507 to $8,519 per full service line replacement, the 25th to 75th percentile of project costs in EPA's 7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey (DWINSA), national, 2022 dollars, as used in the final Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). The full range across the 33 projects was $1,248 to $15,837. In Providence, the public side alone averaged $4,800 and the owner's side about $3,800 (Providence Water 2021, as cited by Marcus).
cost_quote: As described in chapter 4, section 4.2.2.2 of the final LCRI Economic Analysis (USEPA, 2024a), the EPA uses the 25th and 75th percentile values to provide a range of national costs for the final LCRI that reflect the degree of uncertainty in the average service line replacement unit cost ($6,507 and $8,519 for a full service line replacement).
research_notes: Not proposed by the mapping step; included because the group ask lists it (new key). Marcus's valuation: 'Using the average home sales price of $238,000, this suggests a valuation of about $16,000 to $19,000 per public-side LSLR, which is about three to four times as large as the average cost of a public-side replacement, $4,800 (Providence Water, 2021).' Most replacements were partial, since only 1-2 percent of owners also replaced their side. DC information shock, Jiang (2022) job-market paper (https://sites.asit.columbia.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/18/2022/09/JMP-1.pdf): 'neither a difference-in-differences model nor a repeat sales model captures a significant divergence between housing prices of the two types of properties after the release, implying the housing market response to the information was limited.' LCRI: 'Buildings and homes built before 1986 often have LSLs connecting their plumbing system to the main water supply line under the street.' ACS B25034 bins (1980-1989) straddle 1986, so use the pre-1980 share as the proxy. EPA's national estimate (Nov 2025 DWINSA fact sheet, https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2025-11/fact-sheet-2025-7th-dwinsa-update.pdf): 'With the latest data from 2025, EPA estimates that there are 4 million lead service lines across the country.'

name: Fix-It-First home repair grants for low-income owners (Philadelphia BSRP model)
trigger: Tract or block group with many low-income owner-occupants in old homes: HUD CHAS owner households at or below 50% (or 80%) of HUD area median family income (HAMFI) with at least one housing problem, an ACS B25035 median year built before about 1960, and a high owner share (B25003). Strongest fit in shrinking areas (pop2020 < pop2010) where owners cannot recoup repair costs through resale. Thresholds are my proposals.
trigger_data: (1) HUD CHAS (Comprehensive Housing Affordability Strategy) custom ACS tabulations, 2018-2022, released Dec 23, 2025, at tract and other summary levels; public download and query tool at https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/cp.html. (2) ACS 2020-2024 5-year B25035 (median year built), B25034 and B25003 by block group (www2.census.gov summary files, Jan 2026; public).
effect: Home values: none measured. Safety (Philadelphia, 2006-2013, 13,632 repaired homes on 6,732 block faces, compared with waitlisted blocks): each additional home on a block face that received a Basic Systems Repair Program (BSRP) repair was associated with 21.9% fewer total crimes, including assault -19.0%, robbery -22.6% and homicide -21.9%. The effect grew with the number of repaired homes on the block.
effect_source: South, E.C., MacDonald, J., Reina, V. (2021). Association Between Structural Housing Repairs for Low-Income Homeowners and Neighborhood Crime. JAMA Network Open 4(7):e2117067.
effect_quote: The main regression analysis demonstrated that the addition to a block face of a property that received a BSRP intervention was associated with a 21.9% decrease in the expected count of total crime (incidence rate ratio [IRR], 0.78; 95% CI, 0.76-0.80; P < .001), 19.0% decrease in assault (IRR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.79-0.84; P < .001), 22.6% decrease in robbery (IRR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.75-0.80; P < .001), and 21.9% decrease in homicide (IRR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.71-0.86; P < .001).
cost: Up to $20,000 per home: the BSRP grant cap during the 2006-2013 study period, Philadelphia. Covers free electrical, plumbing, heating and roofing repairs, done by city contractors and run by the Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation (PHDC).
cost_quote: The BSRP intervention includes a grant of up to $20 000 provided to low-income owners for structural repairs to electrical, plumbing, heating, and roofing damage.
research_notes: Not proposed by the mapping step; included because the group ask lists Fix-It-First and BSRP (new key). It differs from the existing blight_rehab type, which rehabs vacant homes. Program facts from the paper: 'Operational since 1995, the BSRP is funded by the City of Philadelphia and run by the Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation'; 'The waiting time from enrollment to receipt of BSRP intervention has been 2 to 3 years.' Dose-response: 'A significant dose-dependent decrease in total crime was found such that the magnitude of association increased with higher numbers of homes participating in the BSRP on a block.' The current PHDC page (https://phdcphila.org/repair/basic-systems-repair-program/) says 'The Basic Systems Repair Program (BSRP) provides free repairs to correct electrical, plumbing, heating, limited structural and carpentry, and roofing emergencies in eligible owner-occupied homes in Philadelphia.' It lists a maximum household income of $122,700 for a family of 4 and states no grant cap. No evaluation was found of code enforcement paired with repair, or of home-repair grants' effect on home values.

name: Clean and green vacant lots (shrinking-city trigger for the existing type)
trigger: pop2020 < pop2010 AND other_vacant_share >= 0.10 (ACS) or, where parcel data exist, vacant land above about 3% of the area. In Philadelphia, a vacant-land share above 3% deepens the price penalty from vacancy, and greening there 'effectively eliminates this negative impact'; the city average was 5.8%.
trigger_data: (1) ACS 2020-2024 5-year B25004 and B25001 by block group (www2.census.gov summary files dated Jan 2026; API key needed; public). (2) 2010 and 2020 P.L. 94-171 P1 and H1 by block group with the 2020-to-2010 relationship file (public). (3) Local assessor parcel land use for vacant-land share; there is no national open dataset.
effect: Philadelphia LandCare (Pennsylvania Horticultural Society, PHS): homes within 1,000 ft of a greened lot gain about 4%, rising from 4.3% after year 1 to 13% after 6 years before tapering. The gain is 9% at the city-average 5.8% vacant-land share and peaks at 19% in high-vacancy neighborhoods. Safety, from a randomized trial of 541 Philadelphia lots over 38 months: in neighborhoods below the poverty line, crime fell 13.3%, gun violence 29.1%, burglary 21.9% and nuisances 30.3%.
effect_source: Lin, D., Jensen, S.T., Wachter, S. (2022). The Price Effects of Greening Vacant Lots: How Neighborhood Attributes Matter. Working paper dated June 15, 2022, presented at the 2023 AEA/ASSA meeting.
effect_quote: Using data from a longstanding program in Philadelphia, we find that prices for houses within 1,000 feet of a greened vacant lot rise by about 4%, consistent with the literature, with the effect size increasing over time. Using the extensive data available in Philadelphia, we show how these effects vary by the attributes of the neighborhood in which they occur, with larger effects in areas with a high share of vacant land and higher-than-average median household incomes, with peak responses estimated at 19% and 15%, respectively.
cost: About $5 per square meter (about $0.46 per sq ft) to clean and green a lot, plus about $0.50 per square meter per year to maintain it (Philadelphia, PHS treatment, as reported by Branas et al. 2018).
cost_quote: This intervention has been shown to be inexpensive and highly cost-effective (32), with initial costs averaging about $5 per square meter and maintenance averaging $0.50 per square meter thereafter (33).
cost_check: failed: About $5 per square meter (about $0.46 per sq ft) to clean and green a lot, with maintenance 'averaging $0.50 per square meter thereafter' (Philadelphia; Branas et al. 2018, citing Bonham & Smith 2008). The paper gives no time unit for the maintenance figure, so drop 'per year' unless another source supports it.
research_notes: Existing catalog type (vacant_lot_green); added here for the shrinking-city trigger and newer evidence. From the same working paper: 'In our city-wide results, we find a positive and significant impact of vacant land conversion on the value of nearby properties (within 1,000 feet), with a 4.3% rise in value after the first year, and 13% after 6 years (which then attenuates).' And: 'we estimate a 9% greening effect evaluated at the 5.8% city average level of the vacant land share, with the effect peaking at 19% for high-vacancy neighborhoods.' Safety randomized trial, Branas et al. (2018), PNAS 115(12):2946-2951: 'Significant reductions in crime overall (−13.3%, P < 0.01), gun violence (−29.1%, P < 0.001), burglary (−21.9%, P < 0.001), and nuisances (−30.3%, P < 0.05) were also found after the treatment of vacant lots in neighborhoods below the poverty line.' In Youngstown (Kondo et al. 2016), stabilized lots showed the most consistent drop in burglaries. Heckert & Mennis's (2012) 5.6% estimate is cited by Lin et al.; I did not open the original, and the HUD Cityscape PDF link returned 404.

name: Keep the rural hospital or emergency room open (operating support)
trigger: Block group in a nonmetro county (USDA ERS 2023 Rural-Urban Continuum Code 4-9) whose nearest hospital with an emergency department is the only one within a 30-minute drive. The hospital is a CMS Hospital General Information row with Emergency Services = Yes and type Critical Access, Acute Care or Rural Emergency Hospital. Drive time is computed on OpenStreetMap roads from the block group's population-weighted center. The case is strongest when it is the county's only hospital: the measured income and job losses happen only when the sole hospital closes.
trigger_data: CMS Provider Data Catalog, Hospital General Information (dataset xubh-q36u), https://data.cms.gov/provider-data/dataset/xubh-q36u. Covers every Medicare-registered hospital nationally, with address, county, hospital type and an Emergency Services yes/no field. Metadata modified 2026-07-22, released 2026-08-13. The current CSV has 5,419 rows: 1,382 Critical Access Hospitals, 43 Rural Emergency Hospitals, and 4,495 rows with emergency services. U.S. government data with access level 'public'; no license is named. There are no coordinates, so addresses must be geocoded. Nonmetro test: USDA ERS 2023 Rural-Urban Continuum Codes, https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/rural-urban-continuum-codes (county level; page updated 12/30/2025; based on the 2023 OMB metro delineation; free download).
effect: Home values: no price effect measured. Across 100+ rural hospital closures in 2005-2017, county housing markets did not change: HMDA mortgage originations, denials, purchases and average loan amounts all held steady. Health-care employment fell sharply and stayed down (Alexander & Richards 2023). Other measured effects: closing a county's only hospital cut per-capita income by $703 (1990 dollars), or 4%, and raised unemployment 1.6 percentage points. Closures where another hospital stayed open had no long-run effect (Holmes et al. 2006, 1990-2000 closures). In California, rural closures raised inpatient mortality for time-sensitive conditions by 0.78 points (8.7%); urban closures had no measurable effect (Gujral & Basu, NBER working paper 2019).
effect_source: Diane Alexander and Michael R. Richards, 'Economic consequences of hospital closures,' Journal of Public Economics vol. 221 (2023). The same abstract was read on NBER Working Paper 29110 (July 2021, revised January 2023) and on the RePEc/IDEAS record of the journal article.
effect_quote: We find sharp and persistent reductions in employment, but these localize to health care occupations and are more impactful in areas experiencing complete closures. Aggregate consumer financial health and housing markets appear unaffected by the shuttering of a rural hospital.
cost: $295,051.54 per month per Rural Emergency Hospital in calendar 2026, paid in 12 monthly installments: about $3.54 million a year (my multiplication). Every REH gets the same amount regardless of size. This is Medicare's extra facility payment when a struggling rural hospital becomes a 24/7 emergency-and-outpatient Rural Emergency Hospital, on top of payments for outpatient services. National, 2026; the CY 2025 amount was $285,625.90.
cost_quote: You get additional facility payments in 12 monthly installments. [...] The CY 2026 REH facility monthly payment amount is $295,051.54 with the sequestration amount deducted.
research_notes: Cost source: CMS MLN Fact Sheet MLN2259384 (December 2025), which also says 'The additional monthly facility payment for every REH is the same.' The REH payment prices a 24-hour ER without inpatient beds. Keeping full inpatient service relies on Critical Access Hospital cost-based Medicare payment plus local support, which this research did not price. Holmes, Slifkin, Randolph & Poley, Health Services Research 41(2):467-485 (2006), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1702512/: 'Results indicate that the closure of the sole hospital in the community reduces per-capita income by $703 (p<0.05) or 4 percent (p<0.05) and increases the unemployment rate by 1.6 percentage points (p<0.01).' Gujral & Basu, NBER Working Paper 26182, https://www.nber.org/papers/w26182: 'However, estimating differential impacts shows that rural closures increase inpatient mortality by 0.78% points (an increase of 8.7%), whereas urban closures have no measurable impact.' Alexander & Richards measure housing-market activity (HMDA loan counts and loan sizes), not sale prices. Pharmacy closures were not researched. Grocery is split out as rural_grocery.

name: New or upgraded fire and EMS station (incl. volunteer department support)
trigger: Homes more than 5 road miles from the nearest fire station, the ISO Public Protection Classification line beyond which property is rated Class 10. Distance is measured over OpenStreetMap roads from station points. Also flag block groups whose nearest department is all-volunteer (USFA Dept Type = Volunteer). The USFA registry has no service-area boundaries, so coverage has to be approximated from station or headquarters locations.
trigger_data: U.S. Fire Administration National Fire Department Registry, https://apps.usfa.fema.gov/registry/download. Two CSVs: (1) a national list, which per the page includes all 50 states and U.S. territories; the file downloaded 10 Nov 2026 has 27,117 departments with headquarters address, county, number of stations and Dept Type (18,952 Volunteer, 4,166 Mostly volunteer, 2,606 Career, 1,393 Mostly career); (2) a station list with station addresses for departments that supplied them. Registration is voluntary and the lists are continuously updated. Federal public data; no license is stated. Addresses must be geocoded. Station points can be filled in from OpenStreetMap amenity=fire_station (ODbL 1.0, https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright).
effect: Home values: house values fell at least 6.7% in the year after a community voted to cut fire protection funding. The study is a regression discontinuity comparing fire districts that barely passed or barely failed a fire levy renewal. Cuts larger than the median 18.8% funding drop brought bigger price drops, and the drop did not persist (Brasington & Parent 2024). Insurance: the Texas Department of Insurance says any building more than five road miles from a fire station gets a PPC score of 10, and that premiums generally fall when a community's PPC score improves. It gives no dollar amount.
effect_source: David M. Brasington and Olivier Parent, 'Fire protection services and house prices: A regression discontinuity investigation,' Regional Science and Urban Economics vol. 105 (2024), article 103984. Abstract read on its RePEc/IDEAS record.
effect_quote: House values drop at least 6.7 % the year after a community votes to cut fire protection funding, which is a quarter of a standard deviation of sale price and larger than the capitalization of crime, school quality, or environmental quality. Tax levies representing more than the median 18.8 % funding drop elicit a larger drop in house prices.
cost: About $1.74 million per fire station project (my division). FEMA's 2009 Recovery Act fire station construction grants paid to modify, upgrade or build non-federal stations, with no local cost share. As of 1 Oct 2010 they totaled $207.461 million across 119 awards. National figure in 2009-2010 dollars, not inflation-adjusted, and it mixes new stations with upgrades.
cost_quote: As of October 1, 2010, 119 SCG grants were awarded, totaling $207.461 million to fire departments within the United States.
research_notes: Cost source: Congressional Research Service report RL32341, 'Assistance to Firefighters Program: Distribution of Fire Grant Funding' (3 Jan 2011), read on the EveryCRSReport copy. It also says 'There is no cost share requirement for SCG grants' and that the Recovery Act 'provided an additional $210 million in firefighter assistance grants for modifying, upgrading, or constructing state and local non-federal fire stations', with a $15 million cap per grant. The figure is old. A current local bid or a USDA Rural Development Community Facilities award would be better, but rd.usda.gov refused automated access. Trigger rule source: Texas Department of Insurance PPC FAQ, https://tdi.texas.gov/Fire/fmppcfaq.html: 'Any building more than five road miles from a fire station or outside the boundary of a city or volunteer fire department service area has a PPC score of 10.' and 'If a community’s PPC score improves, insurance premiums will generally decrease.' The Brasington & Parent abstract does not name the state and does not say the districts are rural. It measures the price effect of losing fire funding, not of building a new station.

name: Trailheads, river access and campgrounds
trigger: Rural block group (outside 2020 Census urban areas) within 10 miles of open-access public land (PAD-US Public Access = Open Access) or a river or lake (OpenStreetMap waterway=river or natural=water), with no trailhead (highway=trailhead), boat launch (leisure=slipway) or campground (tourism=camp_site) mapped within that distance.
trigger_data: USGS Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US) 4.1, https://doi.org/10.5066/P96WBCHS. Released March 2025, the most recent version per the USGS PAD-US data-history page. National, with public-access, manager and designation fields. The service metadata carries a liability disclaimer and advises using agency data for single-agency questions. Rural/urban split: 2020 Census urban areas, https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/guidance/geo-areas/urban-rural.html (TIGER/Line, public). An urban area needs at least 2,000 housing units or 5,000 people; everything else is rural. Rivers, lakes and existing facilities: OpenStreetMap, ODbL 1.0 (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright).
effect: Home values: a review of 20 hedonic studies found that homes near trails typically sold for 3% to 5% more than comparable homes. The rural premium is probably smaller: in opinion surveys, only 16% of 1,212 residents along 10 rural trails thought the trail raised their property's value, against 47% along 22 urban trails; 6% overall thought it lowered values (Crompton & Nicholls 2019). County level: in 2000, rural recreation counties had median rents of $474, 23% above the $384 in other nonmetro counties, and median household income 10% higher (USDA ERS 2005).
effect_source: John L. Crompton and Sarah Nicholls, 'The Impact of Greenways and Trails on Proximate Property Values: An Updated Review,' Journal of Park and Recreation Administration 37(3): 89-109 (2019). Abstract read on the journal page.
effect_quote: Twenty hedonic analyses were identified and their results showed that proximity to a trail resulted in home prices that typically were between 3% and 5% higher than those of comparable homes in the area.
cost: Rural trailhead: a $406,822.79 federal Recreational Trails Program (RTP) award for the Town of Haysi, VA Riverfront Trailhead, a motorized trailhead with parking, ADA work, amenities and signage (grant started 9/15/2020, completed 1/29/2025). Smaller 2025 awards in the same report: $160,000 for a James River Water Trail boat ramp (Botetourt County, VA) and $96,000 for trailhead improvements (Town of Narrows, VA). RTP pays at most 80% of eligible costs, so total project cost is at least 25% above the award. Virginia, 2020-2025 dollars.
cost_quote: 331M190 Town of Haysi Riverfront Trailhead $406,822.79 9/15/2020 1/29/2025 [...] Scope: Construction of motorized trailhead including parking, ADA enhancements, trail amenities, and signage.
research_notes: Cost source: Virginia DCR, Recreational Trails Program FY25 Annual Report. Table 3 lists completed projects. Table 4 lists 2025 awards, including 'Botetourt County James River Water Trail Last Lock Boat M^ $160,000.00 $160,000.00' (Ramp is on the next line). The report also states: 'The program reimburses up to 80% of eligible project costs up the award amount.' Rural survey sentence from the same abstract: 'However, while 47% of the 2,647 respondents living close to one of the 22 urban trails believed it increased their property’s value, this was believed by only 16% of the 1,212 who resided proximate to one of 10 rural trails.' USDA ERS, Reeder & Brown, 'Recreation, Tourism, and Rural Well-Being,' ERR-7 (August 2005), https://ageconsearch.umn.edu/record/7220/files/er050007.pdf: 'According to Census data in 2000, median monthly rents for housing averaged $474 in recreation counties, 23 percent higher than the $384 median rent in other nonmetro counties (fig. 4).' These county results describe whole recreation economies, not the effect of one trailhead. No rural-specific hedonic estimate was found, and no primary-source cost per campsite.

name: Pave gravel roads
trigger: Public roads that front homes, tagged in OpenStreetMap as highway=residential, unclassified, tertiary or service (access not private) with surface=unpaved, gravel, dirt, ground or compacted, and with buildings or addresses alongside. Prioritize segments carrying about 200 or more vehicles a day (state or county traffic counts): Minnesota data show gravel upkeep costs jump at that level.
trigger_data: OpenStreetMap road network and surface tags (planet file or Geofabrik state extracts), https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright. National, continuously updated, ODbL 1.0 (share-alike, attribution required). Surface is missing on many rural roads, so untagged county and township roads should show as 'surface unknown', not paved.
effect: Home values: no U.S. estimate found. In Acayucan, Mexico, first-time paving of residential streets in outlying neighborhoods was assigned at random. Within two years, property values rose 17% by professional appraisal (land value +72%) and 28% by homeowners' own valuations. The gain built into property values was about as large as the construction cost (Gonzalez-Navarro & Quintana-Domeque 2016). Costs: in Minnesota county data, gravel road maintenance costs rise significantly at about 200 vehicles a day, which the state DOT summary offers as a possible paving threshold (MnDOT/LRRB 2006).
effect_source: Marco Gonzalez-Navarro and Climent Quintana-Domeque, 'Paving Streets for the Poor: Experimental Analysis of Infrastructure Effects,' Review of Economics and Statistics 98(2): 254-267 (2016). Quote taken from the authors' Oxford Department of Economics Discussion Paper 757 (September 2015).
effect_quote: Using professional appraisals, we find that plots increased in value by 0.54 log points (or 72%), representing a 17% increase in property values (the sum of land and structure). According to homeowner valuations, we estimate an effect of street pavement on property values of 28%.
cost: $600,000-$800,000 per mile to grade and pave a road, depending on terrain and the number of drainage structures, versus about $2,000 a year to maintain a well-traveled gravel road (Washington County, Iowa road department; undated county web page, read November 2026).
cost_quote: It costs between $600,000 and $800,000 per mile to properly grade and pave a new road, depending upon the lay of the land and the number of drainage structures. Paving is an expensive alternative when a well traveled gravel road can be maintained for $ 2,000 per year.
research_notes: The effect quote drops a footnote marker after '(or 72%)'. The Mexico study covers streets in outlying urban neighborhoods, not U.S. rural roads. Its journal abstract adds: 'A cost-benefit analysis indicates that the valuation of street asphalting as capitalized into property values is about as large as construction costs.' Threshold source: MnDOT/Minnesota LRRB technical summary 'Making informed decisions on when to upgrade a gravel road' (October 2006), https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/17871: 'Note that at a traffic volume of 200 ADT, gravel road maintenance costs increase significantly.' Cheaper alternative, re-graveling: Washtenaw County (MI) Road Commission, https://www.wcroads.org/faq/unpaved-roads/: 'Applying gravel or limestone to help “lift” a road can cost between $55,000- $65,000 per mile.' The full 2005 LRRB report on mdl.mndot.gov refused automated access.

name: Extend public water and sewer to homes on wells and septic
trigger: Block groups where many households use private wells or septic, from USGS estimates of domestic-well households (2010 block groups) or from homes outside both EPA public water service areas and EPA sewersheds. Limit to homes within about a mile of an existing service-area boundary, where a line extension is plausible.
trigger_data: USGS, Johnson & Belitz (2019), 'Domestic well locations and populations served in the contiguous U.S.: datasets for decadal years 2000 and 2010,' https://doi.org/10.5066/P9FSLU3B (ScienceBase item 5b9fffe6e4b08583a5c2779e). Estimates are based on block groups, by block-group and road-enhanced methods; contiguous U.S. only; published 2019-06-12; USGS public data. USGS built them because 'The 1990 census was the last nationally consistent survey of a home’s source of water'. EPA Public Water System Service Areas, version 3 (March 2026), https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/public-water-system-service-areas: over 44,000 community water systems covering about 99% of the population they serve. Many boundaries are modeled, and EPA disclaims their spatial accuracy. EPA National Sewershed Dataset, https://www.epa.gov/cwns/sewersheds: nearly 17,000 publicly owned treatment works covering about 78% of the 2020 population. Built on H3 hexagons and not authoritative for individual properties.
effect: Home values: no study measures a water or sewer line extension itself. Closest: in Washington County, PA, across the public-water service boundary, groundwater risk from nearby shale-gas wells cut values of well-dependent homes by up to 24% relative to homes on piped water. This is from the NBER working paper (Muehlenbachs, Spiller & Timmins); the published AER 2015 version reports 'large negative impacts' for groundwater-dependent homes. For sewer the sign can flip: in Miami-Dade, 2002-2022, homes on septic sold at a 3.1% premium, credited to lower operating costs (Hardin, Lin & Thibodeau, 2024 draft). Health: North Carolina children in homes on private wells had 25% higher odds of elevated blood lead than children on regulated community water (Gibson et al. 2020). Connecting 10% of North Carolina's well users to community water would prevent an estimated 2,920 emergency visits a year for acute stomach and intestinal illness (DeFelice et al. 2016).
effect_source: Lucija Muehlenbachs, Elisheba Spiller and Christopher Timmins, 'Shale Gas Development and Property Values: Differences across Drinking Water Sources,' NBER Working Paper 18390 (2012). Later published as 'The Housing Market Impacts of Shale Gas Development,' American Economic Review 105(12): 3633-3659 (2015).
effect_quote: We find that proximity to wells increases housing values, though risks to groundwater fully offset those gains. By itself, groundwater risk reduces property values by up to 24 percent.
cost: Water: $36,467 average long-term cost per connection to tie a domestic-well home into a public water system ('physical consolidation'), versus $103,411 per connection for state small water systems (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2024 Cost Assessment, June 2024; statewide model). Sewer: about $15,000 per home for the homeowner's septic-to-sewer conversion where a public sewer is available (Miami-Dade Water and Sewer, current page). That figure does not include extending the main.
cost_quote: Table 18: Average Estimated Long-Term Solution Cost per Service Connection for State Small Water Systems & Domestic Wells [...] Physical Consolidation $103,411 $36,467 $40,794
research_notes: Table 18 columns are State Small Water Systems, Domestic Well, Average. Sewer cost, https://www.miamidade.gov/global/water/septic-to-sewer-assistance.page: 'The septic-to-sewer conversion would cost a homeowner approximately $15,000.' That is an urban county; rural main extensions cost more per home. name: Bring fiber (100/20 Mbps or better) broadband to unserved homes
trigger: Block groups where many broadband serviceable locations lack fixed service of at least 100/20 Mbps (BEAD 'underserved') or 25/3 Mbps ('unserved') in the FCC National Broadband Map availability data. Rural block groups first.
trigger_data: FCC National Broadband Map / Broadband Data Collection, data download at https://broadbandmap.fcc.gov/data-download/nationwide-data. National, provider-reported fixed availability by location, published twice a year. The FCC's 29 Apr 2026 fact sheet (https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-421212A1.txt) cites the 'Availability Data As Of' Jun 30, 2025 release. Terms are not confirmed: broadbandmap.fcc.gov and the FCC help center refused automated access. Location coordinates (the Fabric) are understood to need a CostQuest license, so plan to map at census block or H3 hexagon level.
effect: Home values: homes with access to 25 Mbps broadband sold for about $5,977 (3%) more than similar homes in neighborhoods with 1 Mbps; the rural premium was lower, at $5,099 (Molnar, Savage & Sicker 2019, national sample). Fiber specifically: about 1% in a standard hedonic model, and 2% (Minnesota) to 9% (Texas) with instrumental variables, using 1.7 million sales in Iowa, Minnesota and Texas, 2015-2021 (Whitacre 2024). Remote rural counties: a 10% increase in coverage raised the median house value by $661 at 0.2 Mbps and $232 at 25 Mbps, with no significant effect above 100 Mbps (Deller & Whitacre 2019).
effect_source: Gabor Molnar, Scott J. Savage and Douglas C. Sicker, 'High-speed Internet access and housing values,' Applied Economics 51(55): 5923-5936 (2019). Abstract read on its RePEc/IDEAS record.
effect_quote: Results show that single-family homes with access to a 25 Mbps broadband connection have a price that is about $5,977, or 3%, more than similar homes in neighborhoods with 1 Mbps. The rural premium is lower at $5,099.
cost: About $10,744 per location in West Virginia's approved BEAD plan, which is 93.6% fiber-to-the-premises across 73,091 locations: a $7,466 average BEAD subsidy plus a $3,278 average provider match (NTIA overview updated 11/20/2025; my sum). Across the 33 state BEAD overviews checked, the average subsidy per location ranged from $2,019 (South Carolina) to $21,986 (North Dakota). These averages mix fiber with satellite and fixed wireless.

name: Main Street downtown revitalization program for a small town
trigger: Small town (roughly 2,000-50,000 people, a design choice) in a nonmetro county or small urban area, with a cluster of storefronts along a main street (OpenStreetMap shop and amenity points) and no local Main Street program.
trigger_data: Census Bureau 2020 urban areas and TIGER/Line places (https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/guidance/geo-areas/urban-rural.html; public), plus USDA ERS 2023 Rural-Urban Continuum Codes for nonmetro counties (https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/rural-urban-continuum-codes). Storefront clusters from OpenStreetMap (ODbL). No national file of designated Main Street programs was found; state coordinating programs post their own lists (for example https://www.commerce.nc.gov/main-street-program/designated-communities).
effect: Home values: none measured. Jobs and businesses: pooled across four Midwest states, adopting the Main Street Program had no significant effect on downtown retail jobs or establishments (difference-in-differences). Iowa was the exception, showing the hoped-for gains (Van Leuven 2022). Self-reported network figures (trade source): Main Street America programs reported $5.68 billion of local reinvestment, 6,630 net new businesses, 35,162 net new jobs and 10,556 rehabilitated historic buildings in 2023, or $18.03 of new investment per $1 of program operating spending. effect_source: Andrew J. Van Leuven, 'The Impact of Main Street Revitalization on the Economic Vitality of Small-Town Business Districts,' Economic Development Quarterly 36(3): 193-207 (2022). Abstract read on its RePEc/IDEAS record.
effect_quote: Using a pooled sample of four Midwest states, the author found no significant effect of Main Street Program adoption on downtown jobs or establishments. name: Keep or open a grocery store in a rural food desert
trigger: Rural census tract (tract center outside 2020 urban areas) flagged low-income and low-access at the 10- or 20-mile demarcation in the USDA ERS Food Access Research Atlas. Or a block group whose only grocery store (OpenStreetMap shop=supermarket or grocery) is at risk of closing.
trigger_data: USDA ERS Food Access Research Atlas, https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/food-access-research-atlas. Census tracts; page updated 10/15/2026. Two maps: the SNAP-authorized Retailer Access Map (new in July 2026; straight-line and driving distance) and the Large Retailer Access Map (last updated 2021; next update expected Winter 2026-27). Tract data can be downloaded; USDA public data. The documentation (https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/food-access-research-atlas/documentation) gives 10- and 20-mile demarcations for rural areas.
effect: Home values: no rural grocery-closure study found. Closest: using over one million sales near 159 Walmarts that opened in 2000-2006, prices of nearby houses rose 2-3% within 0.5 mile and 1-2% at 0.5-1 mile (Pope & Pope 2015).
effect_source: Devin G. Pope and Jaren C. Pope, 'When Walmart comes to town: Always low housing prices? Always?' Journal of Urban Economics 87: 1-13 (2015). Abstract read on its RePEc/IDEAS record.
effect_quote: Using a difference-in-differences specification, our estimates suggest that a new Walmart store actually increases housing prices by between 2% and 3% for houses located within 0.5 miles of the store and by 1–2% for houses located between 0.5 and 1 mile.
cost: Opening or renovating a store: about $2.4 million of state grant per store under the Illinois Grocery Initiative's New Stores in Food Deserts program (15 May 2025 awards; e.g., $2,398,989 for a store renovation in Roodhouse, IL). The grant covers construction or renovation plus first-year wages, utilities and initial inventory. name: Retrofit a dead mall or strip center into a town center
trigger: A big retail site that is mostly parking and partly empty. In data terms: an OpenStreetMap shop=mall or landuse=retail polygon of about 10 acres or more, where surface parking (amenity=parking with parking=surface) covers about half the site or more. It must also meet one of two vacancy tests: (a) the census tract's USPS business-address vacancy rate (vacant business addresses ÷ all business addresses, from the HUD-USPS data) is in the top fifth for its county or metro; or (b) at least a quarter of the Overture places inside the polygon are marked operating_status = permanently_closed or temporarily_closed. The acreage, parking-share and vacancy cut-offs are City Pretty's own choices; no source sets them.
trigger_data: (1) OpenStreetMap, via Geofabrik's state extracts. It is updated all the time. License: 'OpenStreetMap is open data, licensed under the Open Data Commons Open Database License (ODbL) by the OpenStreetMap Foundation (OSMF).' (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright). US counts as of 2026-11-09 from Geofabrik taginfo (https://taginfo.geofabrik.de/north-america:us/, API /api/4/tag/stats): shop=mall 5,147 features; parking=surface 733,993; shop=vacant 14,718; disused:shop 12,848. The vacancy tags are too sparse to use on their own. (2) HUD Aggregated USPS Administrative Data on Address Vacancies (https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/usps.html). Census tracts, released quarterly, with vacant and no-stat counts for both residential and business addresses. Terms: 'Under the current agreement with the USPS, HUD can make the data accessible only to governmental entities and non-profit organizations registered as users.' Use is limited to the 'stated purpose' in the sublicense, so raw tract values may not be publishable on an open map. (3) Openly licensed fallback: Overture Maps Places, field operating_status, defined as 'An indication of whether a place is: in continued operation, in a temporary operating hiatus, or closed permanently.' (https://docs.overturemaps.org/schema/reference/places/place/). Licenses vary by source (https://docs.overturemaps.org/attribution/): Meta and Microsoft data are CDLA Permissive 2.0, Foursquare data Apache 2.0, AllThePlaces data CC0 1.0.
effect: +1.43% on average for a home next to a shopping center just after the center is redeveloped. The gain fades quickly with distance and over time. This is from the Netherlands (inner-city shopping centers, difference-in-differences); the abstract does not define 'next to' as a distance. Related US evidence: around an open-air mixed-use shopping center, prices fell within a 'critical radius' and rose beyond it (Kholdy, Muhtaseb & Yu 2014; the radius is not in the abstract). New Walmart stores raised prices 2–3% within 0.5 mile and 1–2% at 0.5–1 mile (Pope & Pope 2015). Among the sources I could open, none measures nearby home values after a US dead mall was converted into a town center.
effect_source: Zhang, Song; van Duijn, Mark; van der Vlist, Arno J. (2020). 'The external effects of inner-city shopping centers: Evidence from the Netherlands.' Journal of Regional Science 60(4): 583–611. doi:10.1111/jors.12473. Abstract read on IDEAS/RePEc and confirmed in the publisher's Crossref record (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1111/jors.12473).
effect_quote: We find the price of a property located next to a redeveloped shopping center increases by 1.43% on average just after redevelopment. Our results indicate that these positive external effects wear off rather rapidly across space and over time.
cost: Public cost on a 52-acre regional mall site in Alexandria, Virginia (approved July 6, 2021): $86 million in city bonds for site preparation and infrastructure, about $1.65 million per acre. On top of that came $54 million in bonds to buy land for a hospital and lease it out. Total planned investment is more than $2 billion, about $38 million per acre, hospital included. Land bought by a public redevelopment agency in Gwinnett County, Georgia: $16.5 million for 23 acres with 293,059 sq ft of retail buildings, about $0.72 million per acre (Sept. 2024); and $11.5 million for the 11.5-acre former Sears site, about $1.0 million per acre (Sept. 2025). All in nominal dollars. I worked out the per-acre figures myself.
cost_quote: City Council also approved the use of $54 million in public bond financing to allow the City to acquire the land for the hospital and lease it to Inova, as well as $86 million in public bond financing for site preparation and infrastructure at the Landmark site and adjacent Duke Street and Van Dorn Street corridors.
research_notes:
Site size and total investment, from the same Alexandria release: 'The 52-acre Landmark site is one of the most desirable large-scale underdeveloped locations remaining inside the Capital Beltway. The project will transform the currently unoccupied mall into a mixed-use, walkable urban village and will propel the revitalization of the West End of the City of Alexandria.' And: 'The plan will result in more than $2 billion in investment in the community, including the new Inova hospital, medical office buildings, for-rent and for-sale multifamily residential units, retail, commercial, and entertainment offerings.'

Gwinnett County, Macy's site (https://www.gwinnettcounty.com/-/news-events/news-releases/news-details/gwinnett-county-acquires-23-acre-macy-s-site-at-gwinnett-place-mall-1): 'The Gwinnett County Board of Commissioners today approved the Urban Redevelopment Agency of Gwinnett County’s purchase of the Macy’s sites at Gwinnett Place Mall, totaling 23 acres, for $16.5 million.'

Gwinnett County, Sears site (https://www.gwinnettcounty.com/-/news-events/news-releases/news-details/urban-redevelopment-agency-of-gwinnett-county-to-purchase-former-sears-property-at-gwinnett-place-mall-1): 'The Urban Redevelopment Agency of Gwinnett County today approved the $11.5 million purchase of the 11.5-acre former Sears site at Gwinnett Place Mall.'

Supporting effects, all peer-reviewed abstracts:
- Kholdy, Muhtaseb & Yu (2014), Journal of Real Estate Practice and Education 17(1): 1–18 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/taf/rjrpxx/v17y2014i1p1-18.html): 'we find that the open-air shopping center has a negative impact on the price of residential properties within a critical radius to the center, and a positive impact on the price of residential properties beyond the critical radius.' So homes right at the edge of a busy new center may lose value.
- Pope & Pope (2015), Journal of Urban Economics 87: 1–13 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/juecon/v87y2015icp1-13.html): 'Using a difference-in-differences specification, our estimates suggest that a new Walmart store actually increases housing prices by between 2% and 3% for houses located within 0.5 miles of the store and by 1–2% for houses located between 0.5 and 1 mile.'
- Pivo & Fisher (2011), Real Estate Economics 39(2): 185–219 (Crossref abstract: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1111/j.1540-6229.2010.00296.x): 'On a 100‐point scale, a 10‐point increase in walkability increased values by 1–9%, depending on property type.' This covers office, retail and apartment values in NCREIF data, not single-family homes.

Not peer-reviewed:
- Cortright (2009), Impresa for CEOs for Cities (https://nacto.org/wp-content/uploads/walking_the_walk_cortright.pdf): 'In the typical market, an additional one point increase in Walk Score was associated with between a $500 and $3,000 increase in home values.' Walk Score is proprietary, so the map cannot use it as a trigger.

name: Walking paths between cul-de-sacs
trigger: A block group in the bottom quarter of US block groups for EPA street intersection density (Walkability Index field D3B_Ranked ≤ 5 on its 1–20 national scale) that also has many dead-end streets in OpenStreetMap (ends of residential, living_street or unclassified ways that join no other street; service roads and driveways excluded). A school (NCES EDGE point), park (OSM leisure=park/playground) or shops (OSM shop=*) must be within 0.5 mile in a straight line of a cul-de-sac end, while the shortest OSM walking route there is at least about twice as long. There must also be a short gap of roughly 300 ft or less to the destination or the next street, across public land or an existing easement; checking this needs parcel data. All distances and cut-offs are City Pretty's own choices.
trigger_data: (1) EPA Smart Location Database v3.0 and EPA National Walkability Index, covering every 2019 Census block group nationwide. The SLD guide describes D3b as 'Street intersection density (weighted, auto-oriented intersections eliminated)', with extra fields D3bao, D3bmm3/4 and D3bpo3/4 counting intersections by type and number of legs. The intersection measures come from 2018 Q4 HERE NAVSTREETS. EPA page (last updated Sept. 8, 2026): https://www.epa.gov/smartgrowth/smart-location-mapping. Downloads: https://edg.epa.gov/EPADataCommons/public/OA/SLD/SmartLocationDatabaseV3.zip and https://edg.epa.gov/EPADataCommons/public/OA/WalkabilityIndex.zip (both last modified June 8, 2021). License: CC0 1.0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) on the data.gov records https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/smart-location-database and https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/walkability-index; the Walkability Index was issued 2021-05-13. Ranked fields come from 20 national quantiles: 'To score block groups, the block groups were placed into 20 quantiles by variable value (quantiles are groupings with equal numbers of records), each containing 5 percent of the total block groups.' (2) Dead ends and walking-route length: OpenStreetMap, ODbL 1.0 (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright). effect: Home values: I found no measurement for adding a path to an existing cul-de-sac. Related home-price evidence points both ways. Portland-area buyers paid more for more connected street networks and shorter dead-end streets, but preferred being 'less connected to the outside' (Song 2002 dissertation; no size given in the abstract). Homes on cul-de-sacs in Savannah, Georgia sold for more than 9% more (Cebula 2009). Safety (the measured effect): more street permeability goes with higher burglary risk, and cul-de-sacs, especially winding ones, have lower risk (Johnson & Bowers 2010, street-segment analysis; the abstract does not name the place). A UK Home Office-funded study of 12 developments (2,193 homes; police-recorded crime 2007–2009) found that cul-de-sacs linked by footpaths ('leaky') had 110% more crime than true cul-de-sacs, and through roads had 93% more (Armitage 2011, unpublished briefing).
effect_source: Johnson, Shane D.; Bowers, Kate J. (2010). 'Permeability and Burglary Risk: Are Cul-de-Sacs Safer?' Journal of Quantitative Criminology 26(1): 89–111 (March 2010). Published abstract read in the U.S. Justice Department's NCJRS Virtual Library (NCJ 230224); the Springer page blocked automated access.
effect_quote: The findings demonstrate that increased permeability is associated with elevated burglary risk, that burglary risk is lower on cul-de-sacs (particularly those that are sinuous in nature), and that the risk of burglary is higher on more major roads and those street segments that are connected to them.
cost: Paved multi-use trail: median $261,000 per mile, average $481,140, range $64,710 to $4,288,520 (42 observations from 11 sources). National data in 2012 dollars, from the UNC Highway Safety Research Center, prepared for FHWA, 2013. By my arithmetic, a 300-ft connector costs about $15,000 (median) to $27,000 (average), and a 500-ft one about $25,000 to $46,000. These figures leave out buying a strip of land or an easement, design, and lighting (a streetlight has a median cost of $3,600 each in the same table).

name: Build missing sidewalks
trigger: Street segments in OpenStreetMap (highway=residential, unclassified, tertiary, secondary or primary) tagged sidewalk=no, sidewalk:both=no or sidewalk:left/right=no. They count if they lie within 0.5 mile of a school (NCES EDGE point), within 0.25 mile of a transit stop (OSM highway=bus_stop or public_transport=platform, or agency GTFS stops), or within 0.25 mile of shops (OSM shop=*). Streets with no sidewalk tag and no footway=sidewalk way drawn alongside should be shown as 'unknown', not 'missing'. Optionally, rank segments higher in block groups with an EPA National Walkability Index of 10.51 or more ('Above average walkable'), where Li et al. (2015) found larger price gains. The distance cut-offs are City Pretty's choices. FHWA and the City of Tampa both prioritize school zones and transit but give no distances.
trigger_data: OpenStreetMap, ODbL 1.0 (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright), updated all the time and downloadable as daily Geofabrik state extracts. Tags are defined on the wiki (https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Key:sidewalk): sidewalk=no means 'There is no sidewalk at all.'; sidewalk:both/left/right give each side; sidewalk=separate means the sidewalk is drawn as its own highway=footway + footway=sidewalk way. US tag counts as of 2026-11-09 (Geofabrik taginfo, https://taginfo.geofabrik.de/north-america:us/): sidewalk=no 362,528 ways; sidewalk:left=no 339,534; sidewalk:both=no 75,133; any sidewalk=* tag 761,239 ways; footway=sidewalk 4,429,429 ways. For comparison there are 9,232,894 highway=residential ways, so coverage is partial and patchy. Schools: NCES EDGE school geocodes, 2023–24 to 2025–26 (https://nces.ed.gov/programs/edge/Geographic/SchoolLocations; federal, no license stated). Walkability ranking: EPA National Walkability Index, CC0 1.0 (https://edg.epa.gov/EPADataCommons/public/OA/WalkabilityIndex.zip).
effect: Home values: small where streets are car-dependent. Austin, Texas, 2010–2012 single-family sales, spatial hedonic model: adding sidewalks in car-dependent neighborhoods gave only a minimal price increase, and sidewalks and amenities raise prices more in neighborhoods that are already walkable (Li et al. 2015). The abstract gives no dollar or percent figure. Safety: sidewalks cut crashes involving pedestrians walking along roadways by 65–89% (FHWA Proven Safety Countermeasures, from a 2005 Florida DOT study).
effect_source: Li, Wei; Joh, Kenneth; Lee, Chanam; Kim, Jun-Hyun; Park, Han; Woo, Ayoung (2015). 'Assessing Benefits of Neighborhood Walkability to Single-Family Property Values: A Spatial Hedonic Study in Austin, Texas.' Journal of Planning Education and Research 35(4): 471–488. doi:10.1177/0739456X15591055. Abstract read in the publisher's Crossref record; the SAGE page blocked automated access.
effect_quote: Results show that improving walkability through increased access to amenities in car-dependent neighborhoods does not appear to increase property values; adding sidewalks in these neighborhoods leads to a minimal increase in property values. Investments in neighborhood amenities and sidewalks will yield a greater home price increase in a walkable neighborhood than in a car-dependent neighborhood.
cost: About $750,000 per mile of new sidewalk, including engineering design, survey and construction (City of Tampa, Florida). The page was updated April 13, 2026, but the same passage cites 2022 budget conditions, so the dollar year is unclear. Tampa says its roughly 1,300 miles of gaps would cost $975 million. National construction-only bid data, 2012 dollars: concrete sidewalk median $27 per linear foot (average $32; 164 observations from 46 sources). By my arithmetic that is about $143,000 to $169,000 per mile for one side of the street (UNC Highway Safety Research Center for FHWA, 2013).
cost_quote: The average cost to construct new sidewalks is about $750,000 per mile which includes engineering design, survey, and construction.
research_notes:
Safety source: FHWA, Proven Safety Countermeasures: Walkways, FHWA-SA-21-047, 2021 (https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/66694). Quote: 'Sidewalks 65-89% reduction in crashes involving pedestrians walking along roadways.' The sheet cites 'Gan et al. Update of Florida Crash Reduction Factors and Countermeasures to Improve the Development of District Safety Improvement Projects. Florida DOT, (2005).' Where to build, same sheet: 'It is important to provide and maintain accessible walkways along both sides of the road in urban areas, particularly near school zones and transit locations, and where there is a large amount of pedestrian activity.'

Tampa's ranking criteria (same page as the cost): 'All new sidewalk construction projects, also known as capital improvements, are prioritized and selected for inclusion in the long-term work program based on criteria such as documented safety needs, ADA issues, and proximity to schools and transit facilities.' Its list also includes 'Proximity to daily needs (e.g. grocery)'.

National bid data (https://www.pedbikeinfo.org/downloads/Countermeasure_Costs_Summary_Oct2013.pdf), table row 'Concrete Sidewalk $27 $32 $2.09 $410 Linear Foot 46 (164)'. Columns: Median, Average, Min, Max, Unit, Sources (Observations). These bid costs leave out right-of-way, drainage and design, which is why Tampa's all-in figure (about $142 per foot) is much higher.

Other home-value evidence:
- Sohn, Moudon & Lee (2012), URBAN DESIGN International 17: 115–128, King County, WA assessed values (copy on floridadep.gov: https://floridadep.gov/sites/default/files/Economic%20Value%20of%20walkable%20neighborhoods%2C%20Sohn%2C%20Moudon%20and%20Lee%2C%202012_0.pdf): 'Second, better sidewalk coverage in their neighborhood was positively related to increasing property values of rental multi-family residential and retail service uses.' and 'In contrast, few measures of the correlates of walking were significantly associated with single-family residential and office property values.'
- Yencha (2019), about 60,000 Ohio sales: nearby shops add to home prices 'only when there also exists access to adequate pedestrian pathing'.
- Cortright (2009), not peer-reviewed, Walk Score: 'It should be stressed that our measure of walkability captures not just the benefits associated with walking but with greater accessibility generally.' So Walk Score premiums should not be credited to sidewalks.

Suggestion: for a home-value map, Li et al. imply ranking missing sidewalks higher where destinations already exist (higher Walkability Index). Safety-led ranking would favor school and transit areas instead.

name: Home repair grants and loans for owners (roofs, porches, systems)
trigger: ACS block group with median year structure built before 1960 (B25035_001E < 1960), owner-occupied share above 50% (B25003_002E / B25003_001E) and median household income below the county median (B19013_001E). Optionally weight by the share built 1939 or earlier (B25034_011E / B25034_001E), where average repair needs are highest.
trigger_data: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2020-2024 5-year estimates, block group, Census Data API https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5 (B25035_001E, B25003, B19013_001E and B25034 confirmed in the 2024 vintage). Free, but every data request now needs a free key (https://api.census.gov/data/missing_key.html: 'A valid key must be included with each data API request.'). Terms of Service (https://www.census.gov/data/developers/about/terms-of-service.html) require the notice 'This product uses the Census Bureau Data API but is not endorsed or certified by the Census Bureau.' and forbid re-identifying respondents.
effect: Home values: none measured for owner repair grants as such. Safety: in Philadelphia (Basic Systems Repair Program, 1 Jan 2006 to 30 Apr 2013, 13,632 homes on 6,732 block faces), each additional repaired home on a block face was associated with a 21.9% lower expected count of total crime on that block face (IRR 0.78; assault -19.0%, robbery -22.6%, homicide -21.9%). Within blocks that ever had a repair, each additional repaired home was associated with -25.4%, and the effect grew with the number of homes repaired.
effect_source: South EC, MacDonald J, Reina V (2021). Association Between Structural Housing Repairs for Low-Income Homeowners and Neighborhood Crime. JAMA Network Open 4(7):e2117067, doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2021.17067 (PMC9435958)
effect_quote: The main regression analysis demonstrated that the addition to a block face of a property that received a BSRP intervention was associated with a 21.9% decrease in the expected count of total crime (incidence rate ratio [IRR], 0.78; 95% CI, 0.76-0.80; P < .001)
cost: Average estimated cost of needed repairs per owner-occupied home that has repair needs, United States, 2024 dollars: $4,274 (median $2,031) for all owner units; $4,506 for homes built 1940-1969; $5,228 for homes built 1939 or earlier; $5,886 for owners below the poverty line. Program cap example: Philadelphia's BSRP grants go up to $20,000 per home.

name: Proactive, fair code enforcement paired with repair help
trigger: Block group with renter-occupied share above 50% (B25003_003E / B25003_001E) and median year built before 1970 (B25035_001E), or high long-term vacancy (HUD-USPS addresses vacant 90 days or more, tract level, where a licensed user has access; open fallback is ACS vacancy B25002_003E / B25001_001E). Rochester's model applied to rental units built before 1978, with a 'high-risk area' made of the census block groups that held at least 90% of the prior 5 years' elevated-blood-lead inspections.
trigger_data: ACS 2020-2024 5-year estimates (B25003 tenure, B25035 median year built, B25034 year built, B25002 occupancy), block group, Census Data API https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5 (free key required; attribution notice required). HUD Aggregated USPS Administrative Data on Address Vacancies, quarterly, census tract, https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/usps.html: 'Under the current agreement with the USPS, HUD can make the data accessible only to governmental entities and non-profit organizations registered as users.' It cannot be republished on a public map, so use it only as an internal check.
effect: Proactive rental inspection for lead hazards (Rochester, NY, law adopted 2005, rentals built before 1978): among tested children, the share with elevated blood lead (10 µg/dL or more) fell from 8.3% two years before the law took effect to 4.4% two years after (p = 0.027). 94% of inspected units passed interior visual inspections in the first four years. Home values: the authors found no significant effect on the housing market (no price effect measured).
effect_source: Korfmacher KS, Ayoob M, Morley R (2012). Rochester's Lead Law: Evaluation of a Local Environmental Health Policy Innovation. Environmental Health Perspectives 120(2):309-315, doi:10.1289/ehp.1103606 (PMC3279433)
effect_quote: It is reassuring to note that the prevalence of EBL among children tested in Rochester declined from 8.3% 2 years before implementation to 4.4% 2 years after implementation (p = 0.027)
cost: The city's added cost was about $600,000 a year (four new inspectors, administration and dust-wipe analysis) for about 16,500 planned inspections a year, roughly $36 per unit inspected (derived). Landlords' mean repair cost to comply was $1,726 per unit (median $300). Rochester, NY, 2006-2010.
cost_quote: These inspectors, additional administrative needs, and analysis of lead dust wipes cost approximately $600,000 per year. ... The mean per unit cost of repairs was $1,726 (median, $300).

name: Down-payment and homeownership assistance
trigger: Block group with renter-occupied share above 60% (B25003_003E / B25003_001E) and median home value below about 4 times median household income (B25077_001E / B19013_001E < 4). Where the block-group value is suppressed, use the tract or county value.
trigger_data: ACS 2020-2024 5-year estimates B25003, B25077_001E and B19013_001E (confirmed in the 2024 vintage), block group, Census Data API https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5 (free key required; notice 'This product uses the Census Bureau Data API but is not endorsed or certified by the Census Bureau.').
effect: Spillover to neighbors: each housing unit that switches from renting to owning creates about $1,300 in total measured benefits, in the form of higher surrounding home values (U.S., American Housing Survey clustered-neighborhood subsample; instrumental-variable, switching-regression and panel estimates). No study of down-payment grants' effect on nearby prices was found.
effect_source: Coulson NE, Li H (2013). Measuring the external benefits of homeownership. Journal of Urban Economics 77:57-67 (abstract on IDEAS/RePEc)
effect_quote: Estimates indicate that a housing transition from renting to owning creates approximately $1300 in measured benefits.
cost: Philadelphia's Philly First Home grant: up to $10,000 per first-time buyer, or 6% of the purchase price if lower (current program page, 2026). The average sales price of assisted homes is $193,300.
cost_quote: We are offering a homebuyer assistance grant of up to $10,000 (or 6% of the home’s purchase price, whichever is lower) to assist first-time homebuyers reduce the principal, cover down payment, and loan closing costs.
research_notes: Run by PHDC (Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation) for the City. Buyers must complete City-funded one-on-one housing counseling before signing an agreement of sale and must meet income limits (1-person maximum $85,900 on the page). Coulson and Li's $1,300 is the total spillover per conversion, not the gain per neighboring home.

name: Concentrated block investment (Neighborhoods in Bloom, Milwaukee TIN)
trigger: Block group with median home value below the county median (B25077_001E) but housing vacancy under about 10% (B25002_003E / B25001_001E, or HUD-USPS where licensed), and an anchor within about 400-800 m: a public school (NCES EDGE point), a park (PAD-US 4.1 or OpenStreetMap leisure=park), or a rail or frequent-bus stop (the map's GTFS layer). Richmond concentrated spending on 7-to-12 square-block target areas.
trigger_data: ACS 2020-2024 5-year estimates, block group (Census Data API https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5; free key and attribution notice). name: Replace lead service lines and remove lead paint
trigger: Block group where most homes were built before 1980 (B25034_007E through B25034_011E over B25034_001E). ACS year bins do not split at 1986, the year lead pipes were banned. Weight up blocks with many homes built before 1950 (B25034_010E + B25034_011E), or where the water utility's service-line inventory lists lead or galvanized-requiring-replacement lines.
trigger_data: ACS 2020-2024 5-year estimates B25034 (Year Structure Built), block group, Census Data API https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5 (free key; attribution notice). EPA 7th DWINSA lead service line estimates by state, 2025 update (https://www.epa.gov/dwsrf/epas-7th-drinking-water-infrastructure-needs-survey-and-assessment; November 2025 fact sheet: 4 million lead lines nationwide). Address-level inventories are published by each water system under the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions; there is no single national file. Federal data.
effect: Providence, RI (about 10,000 public-side lead service lines replaced 2007-2010): homes whose public-side line was replaced sold for 7-8% more (about $16,000-$19,000 at the $238,000 average price), children's blood lead fell by about 0.4 µg/dL, and renters became more likely to move out. Lead paint: in Charlotte, NC, each $1 of HUD-funded remediation produced $2.60 in benefits, measured through home values (Billings and Schnepel 2017). Nationally, lead paint hazard control returns $17-$221 in health and social benefits per $1 (Gould 2009).
effect_source: Marcus M (July 22, 2023). Burying the Lead: Effects of Public Lead Service Line Replacements on Blood Lead Levels and Property Values. NBER conference paper f186709, Vanderbilt University and NBER
effect_quote: Replacements significantly reduced child blood lead levels by about 0.4 µg/dL, increased property values by 7-8 percent, and increased the probability of moving among renters.
cost: U.S. (EPA 7th DWINSA, 2021 dollars, full and partial replacements): $5,328 (25th percentile) to $9,015 (75th percentile) per lead service line. Providence: the public-side replacement averaged $4,800 and the owner's side about $3,800 (Marcus 2023). Lead paint: $1,200 per housing unit for screening and interim controls, $10,800 for full abatement (Gould 2009, citing the President's Task Force, 2000).
cost_quote: The low estimate (25th percentile or 25% of LSLR cost data is below this value) is $5,328/LSL and the high estimate (75th percentile or 25% of LSLR cost data is above this value) is $9,015/LSL.

name: Property-tax relief for long-time owners (anti-displacement)
trigger: Census tract house price index (FHFA) up more than 30% over 5 years (for example 2020 to 2025), in a block group with many long-time or older owners: a high share of owners who moved in 2009 or earlier (B25038_006E + B25038_007E + B25038_008E over B25038_002E) or of owner householders aged 65 and over (B25007_009E + B25007_010E + B25007_011E). Government example rule: Philadelphia's LOOP requires an assessment increase of 50% in one year or 75% in five years, at least 10 years in the home, and income below 120-150% of AMI.
trigger_data: FHFA annual House Price Index for census tracts (developmental index, not seasonally adjusted), annual through 2025: https://www.fhfa.gov/hpi/download/annual/hpi_at_tract.csv (listed at https://www.fhfa.gov/data/hpi/datasets?tab=additional-data); federal data. ACS 2020-2024 5-year estimates B25038 (Tenure by Year Householder Moved Into Unit) and B25007 (Tenure by Age of Householder), block group, Census Data API https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5 (free key; attribution notice).
effect: Relief keeps older owners in place. Using state property-tax relief programs as instruments, a $100 increase in annual property taxes raised the 2-year moving rate of homeowners over 50 by 0.73 percentage points, an 8% increase over the 9% baseline (U.S., Health and Retirement Study). Home values: none measured.
effect_source: Shan H (2010). Property taxes and elderly mobility. Journal of Urban Economics 67(2):194-205 (abstract on IDEAS/RePEc)
effect_quote: The point estimates from instrumental variable estimation using relief programs to generate instruments suggest that a $100 increase in annual property taxes is associated with a 0.73 percentage point increase in the 2-year mobility rate for homeowners over the age of 50. This is an 8 percent increase from the baseline 2-year mobility rate of 9 percent.
cost: Pennsylvania's Property Tax/Rent Rebate program, a statewide circuit breaker: $380 to $1,000 per eligible older or disabled household per year, plus $190-$500 in supplemental rebates for the neediest. A recent round paid $226 million to nearly 376,000 people, about $600 each (derived). From the current program page.
cost_quote: This program provides a rebate ranging from $380 to $1,000 to eligible older adults and people with disabilities age 18 and older. ... Shapiro Administration Announces $226 Million Headed to Nearly 376,000 Pennsylvanians through Expanded Property Tax/Rent Rebate Program
research_notes: Philadelphia LOOP page (https://www.phila.gov/services/payments-assistance-taxes/taxes/property-and-real-estate-taxes/get-real-estate-tax-relief/apply-for-the-longtime-owner-occupants-program-loop/): 'You may be eligible if your property assessment increased by at least 50% over last year, or by at least 75% over the past five years.' and 'Have been living in your home for at least 10 years.'
