name: Childcare center
trigger: More than 3 children under 5 (ACS B01001_003E + B01001_027E, block group or tract) per licensed child care slot in the area, from state licensing capacity data. This is the 'child care desert' definition from the Center for American Progress, as cited by the U.S. Treasury.
trigger_data: ACS 2020-2024 5-year estimates B01001 (Sex by Age; under-5 counts confirmed), block group, Census Data API https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5 (free key; attribution notice). Definition source: U.S. Treasury, 'The Economics of Child Care Supply in the United States' (September 2021), https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/136/The-Economics-of-Childcare-Supply-09-14-final.pdf .
effect: Home values: none measured. Parents' work: when public kindergarten (an implicit child care subsidy) became available, four in ten single mothers with no younger children entered the work force (U.S. Censuses; state kindergarten grants introduced since the mid-1960s). Treasury's review cites a typical U.S. elasticity of maternal employment to care costs of about -0.1: a 10% lower price means about 1% more mothers working.
effect_source: Cascio EU (2009). Maternal Labor Supply and the Introduction of Kindergartens into American Public Schools. Journal of Human Resources 44(1):140-170 (abstract on IDEAS/RePEc)
effect_quote: Using data from five Censuses, I estimate that four of ten single mothers with no younger children entered the work force with public school enrollment of a five-year-old child.
cost: Operating-cost proxy: in FY 2019 the federal CCDF subsidy paid to child care centers averaged $506 per child per month nationally, about $6,070 per slot per year (derived). Family child care homes received $456 and in-home providers $319. No construction cost per slot was found.
cost_quote: Nationally, the monthly subsidy paid to providers by the CCDF was $319 for child home providers, $456 for family child care home providers, and $506 for child care centers.
research_notes: Trigger definition (Treasury): 'The Center for American Progress uses the approximately 75,000 census tracts (defined by the U.S. Census Bureau as encompassing roughly 4,000 people) around the country to identify areas where there are more than three young children for every licensed child care slot.' name: Crime-prevention design fixes on hot-spot blocks (sightlines, lighting, fences)
trigger: Violent crime rate at least twice the county median. At block-group level this works only where the city publishes geocoded incident data (violent incidents per 1,000 residents by block group, compared with the county's block-group median). Nationally, the FBI Crime Data Explorer gives agency-level monthly violent-crime rates per 100,000 (agency, state and U.S.), so flag whole agencies whose rate is at least twice the state's.
trigger_data: FBI Crime Data Explorer API (https://api.usa.gov/crime/fbi/cde/; needs a free api.data.gov key, and DEMO_KEY works for tests). /agency/byStateAbbr/{state} lists agencies with ORI, latitude/longitude and NIBRS start date; /summarized/agency/{ORI}/V returns monthly violent-crime rates per 100,000 for the agency, its state and the U.S. (checked for Philadelphia PD, 2023). Web app: https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/ . No nationwide block-group crime data exists; incidents come from city open-data portals.
effect: New York City public housing, randomized trial (temporary street lights allocated to 40 developments, March-August 2016): after accounting for spatial spillovers, the added lighting cut nighttime outdoor index crimes by at least 36%. The authors project a benefit-cost ratio of about 4 to 1 for permanent lighting. Home values: no direct measure for design fixes. Pope and Pope (2012), using nearly 3,000 urban U.S. ZIP codes in the 1990s, estimate that property values have an elasticity of -0.15 to -0.35 with respect to crime.
effect_source: Chalfin A, Hansen B, Lerner J, Parker L (2019). Reducing Crime Through Environmental Design: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment of Street Lighting in New York City. NBER Working Paper 25798; published in Journal of Quantitative Criminology 38(1):127-157 (2022)
effect_quote: After accounting for potential spatial spillovers, we find that the provision of street lights led, at a minimum, to a 36 percent reduction in nighttime outdoor index crimes.
cost: Permanent lighting upgrade for a whole public housing development of about 700,000 sq ft: $3-4 million up front, or about $200,000 per development per year over 10 years including about $15,000 a year for electricity. The temporary 2016 pilot cost $5,032,632 in total (about $129,000-$258,000 per development per year). New York City.
cost_quote: However, based on the cost of recent permanent lighting upgrades in public housing, the up-front cost of a development-wide lighting upgrade is expected to be between $3 and $4 million for a development of approximately 700,000 square feet, the average size of developments in our study. ... Over a ten-year planning horizon, we estimate that this type of lighting upgrade will cost, on average, $200,000 per development annually.
research_notes: Home-value link: Pope DG, Pope JC (2012), 'Crime and property values: Evidence from the 1990s crime drop', Regional Science and Urban Economics 42(1-2):177-188, abstract at https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:eee:regeco:v:42:y:2012:i:1:p:177-188 : 'The estimated elasticities of property values with respect to crime range from −0.15 to −0.35. Furthermore, zip codes in the top decile in terms of crime reduction saw property value increases of 7–19% during the 1990s.' The elasticity applies to total crime, so a 36% cut in nighttime outdoor crime alone implies a smaller value gain. Benefit-cost, NBER paper: '...we anticipate that the ratio of benefits to the costs of additional lighting would be approximately 4 to 1.' The published abstract (https://ideas.repec.org/a/spr/joqcri/v38y2022i1d10.1007_s10940-020-09490-6.html) confirms the reduction in nighttime outdoor index crimes but gives no percentage. Lighting is the only design element with experimental evidence here; no measured effect was found for sightlines or fencing. Vacant-lot greening (Branas et al.) belongs to the shrinking-city group.

name: Renovate or rebuild the neighborhood public school (school quality capitalization)
trigger: Block group inside the attendance zone of a public school (NCES SABS 2015-16 boundaries, otherwise the nearest NCES EDGE school) whose buildings need repair or replacement according to the district's facility assessment or capital plan. There is no nationwide school-level building-condition dataset; NCES's 2012-13 national survey found that 53% of public schools needed work.
trigger_data: NCES School Attendance Boundary Survey (SABS), 2013-14 and 2015-16 boundaries for more than 70,000 schools, experimental shapefiles: https://nces.ed.gov/programs/edge/SABS . NCES EDGE public school geocodes, 2024-25: https://nces.ed.gov/programs/edge/Geographic/SchoolLocations . Federal data. Building condition is available only from district capital plans.
effect: In a poor urban district (the IDEAS abstract does not name it), school construction raised home prices in affected neighborhoods by about 10%, and reading scores rose 0.15 SD by six years after the new buildings opened. In California, narrowly passing a school facility bond raised home prices immediately, implying that buyers pay $1.50 or more per $1 of capital spending (Cellini, Ferreira and Rothstein 2010). In an attendance-boundary design, parents pay 2.5% more for a 5% increase in test scores (Black 1999).
effect_source: Neilson CA, Zimmerman SD (2014). The effect of school construction on test scores, school enrollment, and home prices. Journal of Public Economics 120:18-31 (abstract on IDEAS/RePEc)
effect_quote: School construction raised home prices in affected neighborhoods by roughly 10%, and led to increased public school enrollment.
cost: About $4.5 million per school: the average need among the 53% of U.S. public schools that needed repairs, renovations or modernization to put their buildings in good overall condition ($197 billion in total), 2012-13.
cost_quote: The total amount needed was estimated to be approximately $197 billion, and the average dollar amount for schools needing to spend money was about $4.5 million per school (not shown in tables).
research_notes: Not on the mapping step's list; added because the group brief asks for school-quality capitalization (Black 1999 and later). Black SE (1999), 'Do Better Schools Matter? Parental Valuation of Elementary Education', Quarterly Journal of Economics 114(2):577-599, https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:oup:qjecon:v:114:y:1999:i:2:p:577-599. : 'I find that parents are willing to pay 2.5 percent more for a 5 percent increase in test scores.' Cost source: Alexander D, Lewis L, 'Condition of America's Public School Facilities: 2012-13', NCES 2014-022 (March 2014). These effects cover whole districts and attendance zones and are paid for by district bonds, not block budgets, so show this as a district-level item.
